articles.summary: Oil Price Forecast — Brent ($113.88) and WTI ($100) Swing on Ras Tanura Fire and Tehran Talks — $120 Target  TradingNEWS
articles.full_text:
Key Points
- Brent fell 1.7% to $113.88 on Tuesday after a fire near Ras Tanura briefly lifted it to $116.12.
- Saudi crude output dropped from 9.5 million barrels per day before the war to 8 million by September.
- U.S. commercial crude stocks fell 3.06 million barrels to 412.5 million, 3% below the five-year average.
Brent crude for December delivery traded at $113.88 a barrel at 11:10 a.m. ET on Tuesday, down 1.7% from Monday’s settlement at $115.81, and slipped below $114 into the New York lunch hour. West Texas Intermediate fell 1.7% to $100.05, sitting just $0.05 above the $100 line. Abu Dhabi’s Murban grade traded at $117.67. The Brent-WTI spread held near $13.75, a premium that reflects how much tighter the waterborne Atlantic and Middle East markets are than the U.S. inland system.
The day’s range tells the story of the market. Brent opened Asia down 0.98% at $114.68 after a weekend of diplomacy, reversed to $116.12 by 6:30 a.m. ET, up 0.3%, after Saudi Arabia contained a fire near its Ras Tanura export terminal, then reversed again to $113.88 as the market leaned on Monday’s Tehran talks. WTI ran from $100.83 in Asia to $102.45 on the Ras Tanura headline and back to $100.05. A $2.35 intraday swing in Brent, driven entirely by two competing Middle East headlines, is the signature of a market priced on risk premium rather than on barrels lost.
The level is still extraordinary. Brent is up 13% in October, 17.8% over the past month and 80% over the past year, sitting $49 above where it traded at this time in 2025. It touched $117 on Friday, October 23, a six-month high and the strongest since May, after a wave of Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia. Brent settled Friday at $116.72 before Monday’s 0.78% decline to $115.81.
The futures curve confirms the physical tightness. The NYMEX WTI curve sits in steep backwardation, with the December 2026 contract near $101.44 and prices declining steadily along the strip to $50.26 by February 2037. Prompt barrels command a premium of more than $50 over decade-out delivery, a structure that only appears when inventories are scarce and buyers will pay up for oil now.
The setup this week runs on three tracks. Houthi attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure continue daily, with Tuesday’s Ras Tanura incident the latest. Diplomacy is moving for the first time in weeks, with Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan holding talks in Tehran on Monday. And U.S. data lands Wednesday: the weekly Energy Information Administration inventory report at 10:30 a.m. ET and the Federal Reserve decision at 2:00 p.m. ET.
The thesis for this forecast is direct. Brent trades in a $108 to $117 range defined by two forces. Physical tightness, with global inventories down 500 million barrels since February and U.S. commercial crude 3% below its five-year average, sets a floor near $108 to $110. Diplomatic progress and the absence of confirmed Saudi supply losses cap rallies near $117. Only a confirmed hit to Saudi export capacity breaks the ceiling.
Ras Tanura Fire Reverses the Early Selloff
The headline that drove Tuesday’s mid-session spike came from the heart of the Saudi export system. In the early hours of Tuesday, Saudi Arabia contained a fire near facilities operated by Saudi Aramco at Ras Tanura, the kingdom’s largest crude export terminal on the Persian Gulf, following an attack in the region. The extent of the damage was not immediately clear. Ras Tanura hosts the kingdom’s main tanker-loading facilities, its biggest refinery and a large complex of storage tanks.
Yemen’s Houthis claimed they had launched a ballistic missile attack on the Ras Tanura refinery and said it caused a fire. Saudi air defenses intercepted and destroyed three ballistic missiles fired toward the Eastern Province, and the Saudi-led coalition said it also downed four drones aimed at the kingdom’s south. Those intercepts came hours after Monday’s Tehran talks concluded, a sign that the diplomatic track has not yet reached the Houthis.
The market reaction was immediate and short-lived. Brent erased an early 1% decline and rose to $116.12, while WTI jumped 0.7% to $102.45. The rally faded within hours as traders weighed the absence of any confirmed damage to export loading against a growing diplomatic push.
Ras Tanura’s significance explains the sensitivity. Nearly all of Saudi Arabia’s crude exports flow through two ports: Ras Tanura on the Gulf and Yanbu on the Red Sea. When the U.S.-Iran war began in February and Iran blocked much of the traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, Aramco redirected the bulk of its exports to the Red Sea coast via the East-West Pipeline. Ras Tanura sits west of the strait, inside the Gulf, and has been struck before in this conflict: an Iranian strike in early March caused several large fires and forced the refinery to close for about a week.
The pattern matters for traders. Every attack on Saudi infrastructure since September has pushed Brent higher on the first move, and almost every one has faded within one to three sessions because no lasting loss of exports followed. The market has learned to price the headline and then wait for confirmation. Tuesday’s round trip from $114.68 to $116.12 and back below $114 is that learning in action.
For the forecast, Ras Tanura is the facility that could change the market. A confirmed hit to its loading berths, rather than a contained fire nearby, would remove a primary export outlet and justify a sustained move above $120. Until then, each attack adds a few dollars of premium that bleeds away within days.
Tehran Talks: A Promise to Keep Talking, Not a Deal
The force that pulled Brent back below $114 was diplomacy. On Monday, October 26, Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman led a delegation to Tehran alongside Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, and Turkey’s intelligence chief, Ibrahim Kalin. The group met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Supreme National Security Council chief Mohsen Rezaei. It was the first high-level contact between Iran and the three countries, which signed the Mecca mutual defense pact in August, since the war drew Saudi Arabia and the Houthis into direct conflict.
The outcome was modest. Iranian state media said the four countries agreed to continue talks aimed at strengthening cooperation on peace and security. Sources described the clearest result as a promise to keep talking rather than any concrete framework. Iranian officials reportedly linked Houthi de-escalation to U.S. approval of a broader regional truce, and the talks touched on a collective course of action should fighting between Iran and the United States resume.
On Tuesday, Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei met Rezaei and said in a statement that the current state of “neither war nor peace” needs to end, while stressing that Iran’s conditions must be met. Those conditions include an end to the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports and U.S. sanctions on Iranian oil exports. Washington’s position remains far apart: Vice President JD Vance said three weeks ago that Iran must reduce nuclear enrichment to end the war.
President Donald Trump said in a Fox News interview on Sunday that he was approaching a decision on whether to strike a deal with Iran or intensify military operations, leaving additional attacks on the table. That binary choice is now the single largest variable in the oil market.
The market’s read is cautious optimism. Brent fell for a second session as traders priced a lower probability of a wider supply shock, but the decline was measured, $1.93 from Monday’s settlement, because the talks produced no mechanism to stop Houthi attacks or reopen Gulf shipping to full capacity.
The implications for oil run both ways. A U.S.-Iran agreement that lifts the port blockade and eases sanctions would return Iranian barrels to the market and remove the Houthi justification for attacking Saudi Arabia. That combination could take $15 to $20 of risk premium out of Brent within weeks. A U.S. decision to intensify operations would push Brent through $117 and toward $120 to $125.
For the forecast, diplomacy is a cap on rallies, not yet a driver of declines. Until talks produce a framework, Brent’s downside stops at the physical floor near $108 to $110.
The Houthi Campaign: Weeks of Attacks, No Confirmed Lost Barrels
The Houthi offensive against Saudi Arabia has been the dominant supply story of October, and its scale is worth mapping. The Iran-aligned group has attacked the kingdom since September, opening another front in the wider U.S.-Israeli war on Iran.
The October timeline is dense. On October 4, a Houthi drone strike hit Aramco’s Khurais oil processing facility, a 1.2 million barrel-per-day plant in the Eastern Province. On October 5, crude flows were reportedly halted after a strike damaged a pumping station east of Riyadh. On October 22, a drone hit near the Shaybah oilfield without affecting operations, followed by a deadly strike on Dammam airport that killed two people. Over the following 48 hours, the Houthis claimed attacks on the Saudi Defense Ministry in Riyadh, King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, an Aramco site in Yanbu and Abha airport. Aramco evacuated its Dhahran headquarters for the first time since the war began, and Washington ordered non-emergency government staff and families to leave Saudi Arabia.
The weekend extended the campaign. On October 24, the group claimed strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, the Rabigh refinery, crude pumping stations and the East-West Pipeline. On October 26, it claimed drone strikes on pipeline pumping stations. On October 27, it claimed the Ras Tanura attack.
The East-West Pipeline is the critical target. It runs 1,200 kilometers from Abqaiq, the world’s largest oil processing facility, to Yanbu on the Red Sea, and its operating capacity was raised to 7 million barrels per day in 2026 to bypass Hormuz. articles.title: Photographer Tom Hegen’s aerial eye reveals the true scale of the critical mineral age - news - Mongabay
articles.summary: Photographer Tom Hegen’s aerial eye reveals the true scale of the critical mineral age  news - Mongabay
articles.full_text:
- As the world shifts to cleaner energy to address climate change, demand is soaring for transition minerals such as lithium, cobalt, nickel, and rare earth elements, used in green technologies.
- Aerial photographer Tom Hegen has spent the past six years documenting where these critical minerals come from, exploring some of the world’s most significant mining regions.
- Hegen’s images reveal in meticulous and beautiful detail the wider landscapes impacted by mineral extraction, highlighting the environmental, social, and geopolitical costs.
- In this interview with Mongabay, Hegen says he hopes his images encourage viewers to look closer and consider how their actions and consumption habits can support greater responsibility, transparency, and accountability throughout global supply chains.
From the air, the vivid lithium fields of Chile’s Atacama Desert look like an intricate computer circuit board, hinting at the technological destination of this increasingly crucial mineral.
Photographer Tom Hegen has spent the past six years documenting some of the world’s most significant mining regions that supply the critical minerals needed for modern technologies and the green energy transition.
Shooting primarily aerial images using small aircraft, drones, and high-resolution cameras, Hegen captures heavily impacted landscapes in meticulous detail. His images depict vast, immersive scenes of the wider consequences of mineral extraction that might otherwise remain hidden from view at ground level: snaking watercourses discolored by mercury, settlements disappearing under piles of mining waste, and coastal sediment plumes smothering artisanal fishing grounds.
“An elevated perspective offers a powerful way to observe, understand, and reflect on how we have transformed the Earth’s landscapes,” Hegen told Mongabay. By creating visually striking images, Hegen said he hopes to encourage people to look more closely.
A prior photographic project documenting the effects of climate change in the Arctic sparked Hegen’s interest in the energy transition and the critical minerals on which it depends.
Although research suggests expanded mining to meet the demands of the energy transition would require less mining overall than the current fossil fuel-based system, Hegen’s work inspires questions about who bears the costs of this shift.
“What particularly caught my attention was that many of these resources are concentrated in just a handful of countries, [and] their extraction often comes with significant environmental and social consequences that receive relatively little public attention,” he said.
Now having spent significant time in the field among ecosystems and communities facing pollution, health risks, and deforestation, Hegen said he’s come to realize that no type of energy comes with zero environmental or social consequences. “The central question is not whether we should pursue the energy transition,” he said, “but how we can make it more sustainable and equitable.”
Mongabay’s Carolyn Cowan interviewed Tom Hegen in October, ahead of the launch of his book The Mineral Age, which features a wide selection of his photography exploring the environmental, social, and geopolitical costs of the transition to green energy.
Mongabay: What led you to spend six years documenting mineral extraction around the world?
Tom Hegen: I initially began photographing coal mining in Germany, while also exploring the visible impacts of climate change. Through this work, I came to understand that decarbonizing our economy would be one of the defining challenges of the current century. As I researched the energy transition more deeply, I found out that low-carbon technologies, along with much of our modern technological infrastructure, depend on vast quantities of minerals such as lithium, cobalt, nickel, and rare earth elements. While we are trying to move away from fossil fuels, the transition requires an enormous expansion in the extraction of these critical minerals.
What particularly caught my attention was that many of these resources are concentrated in just a handful of countries, creating new geopolitical dependencies and vulnerabilities. At the same time, their extraction often comes with significant environmental and social consequences that receive relatively little public attention.
This realization became the starting point for The Mineral Age, a six-year photographic project documenting mining regions around the world that supply the essential raw materials underpinning our technological progress and the transition to a low-carbon future.
Mongabay: As you say, many of the minerals you document are increasingly crucial for developing renewable energies, electric vehicles, and other technologies associated with the energy transition. Has documenting their extraction changed the way you think about the idea of renewable or “clean” energy?
Tom Hegen: Documenting these mining regions has made me realize that moving away from fossil fuels is far more complex than we might initially imagine. At the same time, I have no doubt that decarbonizing our economies and the way we live is essential in order to address climate change. The pressing question, however, is at what cost, and who ultimately bears that cost?
As our societies become increasingly digitalized and technologically advanced, and as we accelerate the energy transition, we will need never-before-seen quantities of critical minerals in the coming decades. What I’ve come to understand is that no source of energy is entirely without environmental or social consequences. Even technologies we consider clean or renewable depend on extensive industrial processes and the extraction of finite resources.
Mongabay: What can aerial photography reveal about the impacts of mining that might escape ground-level observations? And what might it miss that on-the-ground reporting could help reveal more about?
Tom Hegen: The true scale and environmental impact of mining operations are often almost impossible to comprehend from ground level. The aerial perspective allows us to see the bigger picture, revealing how entire landscapes are transformed by extraction, infrastructure, waste deposits, and pollution. It makes patterns, dimensions, and connections visible that would otherwise remain hidden.
Through my photography, I focus on the broader environmental footprint of our collective activities rather than on individual stories on the ground. At the same time, I recognize that there are many different perspectives from which these issues can be explored. Behind these landscapes are countless human stories, particularly those of miners, local communities, and people whose livelihoods and environments have been affected by resource extraction. I see aerial photography and ground-level reporting as complementary approaches, each revealing different aspects of the same complex reality.
Mongabay: Once you began photographing mining landscapes, were you surprised by anything you were capturing in your images that you hadn’t anticipated when you first conceived the project?
Tom Hegen: From my initial research, I knew that many of the so-called critical minerals are found in developing countries, particularly across the Global South. I also anticipated that accessing some of these mining regions would be challenging, as they are often extremely remote, heavily restricted, or shielded from public view. In some cases, such as the Democratic Republic of Congo, it took me more than two years to gain access and photograph the mining sites.
What surprised me most was just how complex the extraction of these minerals is, and the scale of the environmental, social, and political challenges involved. Many of these resources are extracted in regions where environmental regulations are weak or poorly enforced, where child labor remains a serious concern, and where mining operations can have devastating consequences for local communities and ecosystems.
As the project developed, I became increasingly aware of a side of the energy transition that remains largely invisible to those of us living in industrialized countries. We tend to focus on the benefits of clean technologies, but rarely consider where the raw materials come from or the conditions under which they are extracted. Seeing these realities firsthand made me realize just how much of the environmental and social cost of our technological progress is borne by communities far removed from those who ultimately benefit from it.
Mongabay: Do any landscapes or encounters stand out to you in particular?
Tom Hegen: What struck me most was the scale of environmental destruction, particularly in developing and low-income countries. In places such as Indonesia and the Democratic Republic of Congo, mining often takes place under weak or poorly enforced environmental regulations, with severe consequences for local communities and ecosystems. Both large multinational mining companies and local artisanal miners are involved, although they operate under very different circumstances.
One thing I came to realize is that wherever there is a valuable mineral deposit, there is a will to exploit it, even in the most remote corners of the planet, deep within tropical rainforests or beneath the ocean floor.
On Bangka Island in Indonesia, for example, I documented tin mining operations that extract minerals from the seabed, damaging marine ecosystems and threatening the livelihoods of local fishing communities. On the island of Sulawesi, vast areas of tropical rainforest are being cleared to make way for nickel mines and processing facilities, fundamentally transforming entire landscapes. In the Democratic Republic of Congo, I witnessed artisanal miners digging deep underground shafts to extract cobalt, often risking their lives under extremely dangerous working conditions.

articles.full_text:
By Olesya Astakhova and Ahmad Ghaddar
MOSCOW/LONDON, Oct 27 - OPEC+ oil-producing countries are likely to keep their December oil output targets steady on Sunday, three people with knowledge of the matter told Reuters, in line with expectations that further output policy adjustments are unlikely until next year.
The online meeting of seven core OPEC+ members — Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman — comes as Gulf members have been boosting exports that have been disrupted for months by the Iran war. Most, however, are still pumping well below their output targets.
All three people declined to be named and said no final decision had been made.
OPEC+ comprises the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies including Russia. OPEC and authorities in Russia did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Advertisement
In September, OPEC+ completed the phased rollback of a 1.65 million-barrel-per-day supply cut first agreed in 2023. Disruption caused by the Iran war has meant Gulf producers are falling below their quotas.
Reuters reported in July that OPEC+ was likely to make no changes to its targets during the fourth quarter as it turns its focus to 2027 quota negotiations.
The group still has one more layer of production cuts of about 2 million bpd covering most members through the end of 2026.
OPEC+ needs to finalise a review of members' production capacity before setting the 2027 baselines that will determine future quotas and shape plans to unwind those cuts, sources have said.
(Reporting by Ahmad Ghaddar and Olesya Astakhova;Editing by Alex Lawler and Joe Bavier)

articles.title: Critical Minerals Supply Chains Enter a New Phase of Global Competition - Kalkine
articles.summary: Critical Minerals Supply Chains Enter a New Phase of Global Competition  Kalkine
articles.full_text:
Highlights
- The IEA expects critical-mineral demand to nearly double by 2040 under stated policies.
- Lithium demand is projected to grow more than threefold by 2040.
- Copper demand is projected to increase by about seven million tonnes.
- Announced projects have narrowed the projected copper supply gap.
- Refining and processing capacity remain less diversified than mining capacity.
- Trade and industrial policies increasingly influence supply-chain investment.
The global competition for critical minerals is shifting from the discovery of deposits to the ability to process materials into products that manufacturers can use. Copper, lithium, nickel and rare earths are central to electricity networks, batteries, digital infrastructure and industrial technology. Demand is expected to expand over the coming decades, but new mines alone cannot guarantee reliable supply. The International Energy Agency’s 2026 critical-minerals outlook highlights the growing importance of refining, manufacturing and policy decisions.
Latest Policy Moves Put Supply Security Back in Focus
On 23 October 2026, the United States designated helium a critical material, citing its role in semiconductor manufacturing and exposure to international supply disruptions. The move illustrates how industrial security now extends beyond battery minerals to specialist inputs used in electronics, medical equipment and energy technology. Meanwhile, 26 October metals-market reporting showed zinc reaching a two-week high as tight inventories supported prices, even as copper faced pressure from rising exchange stocks and demand concerns. These contrasting developments reinforce the importance of distinguishing short-term price moves from the longer-term concentration of processing and supply chains.
Electrification Drives the Long-Term Demand Story
Under the IEA’s stated-policy scenario, aggregate demand for critical minerals almost doubles by 2040. Lithium is projected to record the strongest increase, with demand rising more than threefold. Nickel, graphite and rare-earth demand is also expected to grow strongly. Electric vehicles, energy storage, renewable generation and electricity grids remain major drivers. The expansion of data centres and other digital infrastructure adds another dimension to mineral requirements.
Copper Occupies a Distinct Position
Copper is central to power networks, electrical equipment and industrial systems. The IEA projects the largest absolute increase in demand for copper among the minerals assessed, adding approximately seven million tonnes by 2040. This does not imply that demand will rise in a straight line: economic growth, construction cycles and investment spending will still affect annual consumption. However, the long-term requirement for grid expansion makes copper supply planning strategically important.
More Projects Do Not Remove All Supply Risk
The pipeline of announced projects has improved the projected market balance for several minerals. The IEA estimates that the copper supply gap in its base case has narrowed from around 30% to 25%, while the outlook for lithium has also improved. These are projections, not confirmed future shortages. Mine approvals, financing, construction timelines and operating performance will determine how much planned capacity becomes actual production.
Processing Remains the Weak Link
New mining projects are being developed across a wider set of countries, but refining and downstream manufacturing remain concentrated. Rare earths illustrate the problem: announced mining capacity outside the leading producer exceeds the capacity planned for refining, separation and magnet manufacturing. Similar mismatches affect lithium and other battery materials. Without processing capacity, a country can mine ore yet remain dependent on overseas facilities to turn it into usable industrial inputs.
Industrial Policy Reshapes Investment Decisions
Governments are seeking to diversify mineral supplies for energy security, manufacturing and strategic industries. Support for domestic processing can encourage investment, but projects must still contend with high capital costs, skilled-labour requirements and competitive international markets. Export restrictions and production quotas can also change expected supply. The IEA notes that the projected cobalt supply gap has widened, reflecting developments in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
What the Next Decade Will Test
The challenge is to develop complete supply chains rather than isolated mining assets. Progress will depend on permitting, infrastructure, electricity costs, financing and the pace at which processing plants reach commercial operation. The balance between diversification and economic efficiency will shape how resilient the next generation of mineral supply networks becomes.
Critical minerals are becoming a strategic macroeconomic priority. Future resilience will depend as much on refining and manufacturing investment as on the volume of minerals identified underground.

articles.title: China’s Rare Earth Tactics Reflect Market Power, Not Manipulation, Study Finds - AZoM
articles.summary: China’s Rare Earth Tactics Reflect Market Power, Not Manipulation, Study Finds  AZoM
articles.full_text:
China controls much of the world’s refined rare earth supply, but determining whether its pricing practices cross into manipulation requires a closer look at how prices are formed.
Paper: Manipulation in the Rare Earth Market? AI-generated abstract conceptual image created using ChatGPT/OpenAI
A recent research paper on SSRN examines whether China’s dominance of the rare earth industry constitutes market manipulation or reflects its industrial policies and control over production. Combining economic analysis, legal rules, and historical price data, the study separates deliberate price distortion from the exercise of market power.
Understanding Market Manipulation in the Rare Earth Industry
Rare earth elements (REEs) play a crucial role in advanced technologies, including electric vehicles, wind turbines, electronics, defense, and aerospace systems. Neodymium and praseodymium enable the production of high-performance permanent magnets, while dysprosium and terbium support applications that require specialized magnetic properties.
Several countries possess rare earth deposits, but China accounts for about 90% of global refined rare earth production.
Decades of investment, processing expertise, industrial consolidation, and government support have helped China establish this dominant position. Its market influence has raised concerns about whether competing producers can remain financially viable. Mining projects outside China often attract investment when prices rise, then struggle to remain profitable when prices fall.
Critics argue that China may deliberately increase supply to depress prices, weaken foreign competitors, and discourage new investment. Price declines alone do not establish market manipulation. The paper also says China kept investing in rare earth capabilities while other countries shifted parts of the supply chain offshore.
The study asks whether China’s rare earth market practices meet the paper’s proposed economic definition of manipulation. It addresses a research gap in the literature that largely examines private traders in regulated financial markets.
The authors note that no single definition of market manipulation is settled in law and economics. China’s rare earth industry combines state influence over production, industrial policy, and ownership interests in pricing infrastructure. The paper uses these distinctions to separate deliberate manipulation from subsidies, production controls, industrial policy, and the exercise of market power.
Assessing Market Conduct Through Economic and Price Analysis
The researchers developed an analytical structure that combines legal precedent, financial economics, industrial policy, and historical market data. It separates violations of existing laws from practices that meet the paper’s economic definition of market manipulation.
The legal analysis asks whether international rules prohibit particular market practices, while the economic analysis asks whether those practices artificially distort prices through the price discovery process.
The authors identify a separate precondition and three dimensions for manipulation: artificiality, intent, and gain. Artificiality occurs when market prices diverge from fundamental value. Intent requires evidence that an actor deliberately creates this divergence, while gain refers to the economic or strategic advantage sought.
Before assessing those three dimensions, the conduct must influence prices through a price discovery mechanism, the process that turns transactions or market assessments into a reference price, rather than simply changing production costs, supply levels, or individual transaction terms.
The study applies this test to China’s export and production quotas, industry consolidation, technology restrictions, and ownership of pricing infrastructure. It also examines these practices under World Trade Organization (WTO) rules and relevant trade and competition rules.
Researchers established two price thresholds to investigate allegations of market flooding. The cost threshold draws on reported production costs from Molycorp and Lynas Rare Earths, using a blended rare earth oxide cost series rather than an NdPr-specific cost. The entry threshold represents the price needed to justify new investment.
The authors anchor that threshold to the US government’s 2025 agreement with MP Materials, which included a 10-year price floor of US$110 per kilogram for neodymium-praseodymium oxide. They compare these benchmarks with historical prices and Lynas’s average selling prices, including the 2010–2011 and 2021–2022 market cycles.
Price Patterns, Industrial Policy, and Market Vulnerability
The analysis indicates that China’s major rare earth market practices do not meet the study’s proposed definition of market manipulation.
Export restrictions, production quotas, industry consolidation, and technology controls influence supply, industry structure, production costs, or competitors’ capabilities. The researchers classify these measures as exercises of market power or industrial policy because the evidence does not demonstrate artificial price distortion through the price discovery mechanism.
China’s export restrictions illustrate this distinction. In February 2011, the gap between domestic and export neodymium oxide prices peaked at 176%. Following a WTO ruling against the restrictions, the median price difference fell to 3.6% in 2015. The researchers conclude that the restrictions discriminated against foreign buyers and violated international trade obligations. That finding does not establish market manipulation.
China’s industry consolidation concentrates quota enforcement and pricing power; production quotas manage supply; and technology restrictions limit competitors’ access to processing expertise and manufacturing capabilities.
China Northern Rare Earth holds a controlling stake of about 40% in the Baotou Rare Earth Products Exchange (BREPE), while other price reporting agencies rely on Chinese producer data and opaque methodologies. This ownership structure creates a vulnerability in price discovery.
The paper argues that without an independent price, artificiality cannot be tested, so ownership alone does not establish manipulation.
The price analysis also challenges claims of below-cost market flooding. Between 2013 and 2020, neodymium-praseodymium oxide prices remained above the paper’s estimated blended cost threshold and below the threshold needed to encourage new investment. This pattern is consistent with limit pricing, which can discourage competitors from expanding capacity without forcing existing producers out of the market.
Lynas operated near break-even during much of this period. Prices exceeded the entry threshold in 2011 and 2021–2022, coinciding with increased investment in non-Chinese production.
The authors warn that the price series comes from Chinese price reporting agencies, creating a methodological problem because the data may itself be influenced by the conduct under investigation. The model cannot distinguish a genuine limit-pricing pattern from one partly produced by compromised price reporting.
The result counts against the flooding claim, yet it does not show that the observed price band is a market outcome or that it reflects fundamental value.
Policy Implications and Market Vulnerabilities
Under the authors' proposed test, the study gives market manipulation a narrow meaning and cautions against using the term as a broad label for aggressive or strategic market behavior.
China’s dominance in rare earth production, industrial policy, and technology restrictions creates significant challenges for foreign competitors. The researchers argue that policymakers should assess these practices under trade and competition law, where applicable, rather than automatically classifying them as manipulation.
The study describes limits on enforcement through international trade rules. A WTO ruling prompted China to remove its export restrictions in 2015, but existing mechanisms still struggle to address its production controls, industry consolidation, and technology restrictions. Weaknesses in the WTO dispute settlement system further restrict efforts to challenge these practices.
Countries seeking to diversify critical mineral supply chains could benefit from independent, transaction-based price discovery outside China.
The authors say such pricing would let reported prices be tested against an independent signal and help external investors assess the risk of committing capital to competing supply.
The researchers also suggest that lower rare earth prices could benefit downstream Chinese industries, including electric vehicle manufacturers. They propose one unproven mechanism: low-cost domestic transfers reported as market activity could make supply appear larger and average prices lower, discouraging foreign entry.
They stress that this is a theoretical proposition. If established, it could fall on the manipulation side of the authors’ test.
The paper proposes a test to distinguish market manipulation from industrial policy and market power. Independent transaction-based pricing outside China would provide an external benchmark for testing whether reported prices diverge from fundamental value.

articles.title: Why Critical Mineral Shortages Are a CEO Issue - Boston Consulting Group
articles.summary: Why Critical Mineral Shortages Are a CEO Issue  Boston Consulting Group
articles.full_text:
CEOs at industrial companies are well aware of potential shortages in critical minerals, and many think they have a plan in place to mitigate those risks. But we consistently find that companies are still underestimating their true vulnerability. Most industrials track their exposure to critical minerals using high-level metrics like spending, information from tier one suppliers, or country-of-origin data. However, true exposure is larger than those metrics suggest. This is because mineral risk often sits deep inside supply chains—inside the components that companies buy, and inside the tools and processes used to make those components. Concentration risks require looking at processing and ownership, not just mineral production at the mine.
A more comprehensive approach can give companies an accurate view of the vulnerabilities in their supply chain. From that baseline, companies can take a range of steps to reduce their exposure. Critically, this approach also helps companies tap into pools of public capital that many countries have allocated. In 2025, public finance commitments to critical minerals in advanced economies reached around $65 billion, more than four times the 2023 level, and most of that money is not yet spent. When companies have a clear sense of their financial exposure, they can build a case to access these funds.
In that way, industrial companies can stop treating critical minerals as a cost item and start treating them as a source of strategic advantage.
Three Blind Spots Understate the Risk
Potential shortages of critical minerals are not new, but the scale of the looming shortfall is striking. In our proprietary model, the demand for key inputs—including rare-earth elements (REEs) and more common products like graphite, copper, and lithium—will be roughly 120% to 250% of forecast supply through 2040. New demand is coming primarily from batteries and electrification (which together are projected to increase the demand for critical minerals 20-fold by 2040), but also from the AI buildout and increased defense spending (segments that are projected to cause demand to triple and quadruple, respectively).
In response, the conventional move is to turn to procurement teams to fix the exposure. But this analysis will not give CEOs the full picture. Leaders need to be aware that the broadly prevailing metrics will lead to three critical blind spots.
Blind Spot 1: Overweighting Dollars Spent. Companies often start their risk assessment by looking at their bill of materials, leading them to worry about materials like copper and lithium that are large in tonnage and in procurement dollars. But the more dangerous exposures are often in “mosquito minerals” that are so small by traded value that they never reach the risk register, yet so essential that entire high-value chains stop without them. (See Exhibit 1.)
For example, REEs comprise roughly 40% of the cost of a magnet but less than 1% of the total value of an electric vehicle that requires the magnet. That is too cheap to appear in any cost review that would flag it as a risk, yet a shortage of these elements can stop a production line.
Similarly, a fighter jet uses about 20 kilograms of REEs, which are worth less in total than the paint that coats the plane. Those minerals are a rounding error in percent of unit cost, yet the aircraft does not fly without them.
Rare-earth elements have been getting a lot of attention lately, but the list of “mosquito minerals” is much longer. Consider the following examples:
- Gallium. The entire global market for gallium is worth less than $350 million a year, with annual production of only about 900 tons—making it negligible compared to most other commodities. Yet we estimate that approximately $3.5 trillion worth of final products depend on gallium, including high-speed logic and power chips, AI GPUs, and 5G and satellite communications components. For many of these applications, substitutes are either not available or are technically challenging, with long lead times.
- Germanium. Global sales of germanium each year only total about $260 million, but it is an essential component of electronics and fiber optics, and AI is hungry for both. A recent series of events—export licensing in 2023 followed by an outright ban on exports to the US in 2024 and a cut-off of Japan in early 2026—created severe market turmoil. Germanium prices during this period roughly quadrupled in western markets, trading at a substantial premium to Chinese volumes.
- Arsenic. Virtually no companies list arsenic as a strategic risk, yet in ultra-high-purity form it is indispensable to the gallium-arsenide (GaAs) semiconductors in 5G/6G telecom infrastructure, along with AI data-center optics, radar systems, and defense electronics. The upstream market is minuscule (about $50 million worldwide), and producing semiconductor-grade arsenic (99.999995% pure, also known as 7N5) takes years of accumulated process know-how, with supply chains highly concentrated. China controls about 90% of refining volume, and a single Japanese producer supplies roughly 60% of the world’s ultra-high-purity arsenic. One facility, in one of the most seismically active countries on earth, and no credible alternatives. That is the problem in its purest form: negligible spend by companies, no risk-register entry, and an entire class of advanced and defense electronics that stops without it.
The economics of “mosquito” minerals has an additional wrinkle: they are often recovered as byproducts from other mining and industrial processes. Their supply is therefore set by the market dynamics of the host metal, not their own. So even a sharp price spike does not reliably call forth new production the way it would for a primary commodity.
Blind Spot 2: Looking Solely at Tier One Suppliers. Companies tend to look at critical minerals in the products and components they buy from their direct suppliers. Yet a company that buys almost no critical minerals directly can still be acutely exposed, because minerals arrive embedded in components. A motor, magnet, power module, laser, or sensor carries upstream mineral content, leading to dependencies that may not appear on a raw-materials line.
Another reason that companies understate risk is that minerals are not only in the product. They are in the processes required to create products: the crucibles, sputtering targets, furnace internals, catalysts, dies and consumables of suppliers’ production lines, and in the capital equipment itself.
For example, turbine blades, engine blocks, and structural aerospace components are machined with cutting tools made of tungsten carbide bonded with cobalt, chosen because no other material holds an edge at the temperatures and speeds that modern precision machining requires. The cutting tools wear down and need to be replaced. Tungsten mining and refining are heavily concentrated in China, which has in recent years tightened export licensing on tungsten products. Cobalt carries its own concentration risk through the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where production is dominated by a small number of foreign operators. A manufacturer that has never bought a gram of tungsten or cobalt directly can still find its production line stopped by a shortage of the tooling that cuts its parts—a dependency that does not show up on any bill of materials.
Blind Spot 3: Focusing on Mineral Production Rather Than Processing and Ownership. Companies map their exposure to where critical minerals are mined. But processing—not production—is the bottleneck for some minerals. For example, China refines roughly 90% of rare earths and holds the know-how to turn ore into usable magnets. Similarly, it processes some 65% to 70% of lithium and cobalt and around 70% of graphite. Australia produces lithium and ships more than 90% of its spodumene to China to be processed.
Some industrial companies are beginning to factor processing concentration into their risk calculus. But another aspect that few companies measure is ownership of those assets. A map of where assets sit and a map of who owns them can look radically different. Consider cobalt and nickel. (See Exhibit 2.)
- Cobalt shows concentration at the mining stage. The DRC accounts for roughly two-thirds of global mined cobalt production, with major operations majority-owned by Chinese companies.
- Nickel shows concentration at the refining stage. Indonesia hosts close to 70% of upstream nickel capacity, while Chinese companies and shareholders account for a majority of Indonesia’s nickel-refining capacity. Moving a supply contract from a Chinese refinery to an Indonesian one may not change a company’s geopolitical risk exposure.
A Missed Opportunity to Access Public Funds
On their own, the three blind spots are bad enough. But they also mean that companies are missing out on valuable capital from public sector vehicles. If organizations don’t know the full scope of their risk, they don’t realize the opportunities they might have to tap into these resources.
In 2025, public finance commitments to critical minerals in advanced economies reached around $65 billion, more than four times the 2023 level. These structures are not free money; they carry conditions—typically reporting obligations, governance rights, localization requirements, and screening. They are also not a full solution. Instead, they’re meant to be a catalyst, reflecting about one-tenth of the overall capital required to meet the demand for critical minerals through 2040. But they are funds that the private sector can tap into to build a competitive advantage.
Thus far, the vast majority of this capital has been committed but not yet spent. articles.summary: ARM backs R16bn mining expansion and nickel mine restart  Business Day
articles.full_text:
African Rainbow Minerals (ARM) will spend almost R16bn to expand its platinum group metals (PGM) operations and restart its Nkomati Nickel Mine, as the diversified miner looks to increase production amid differing conditions across its commodity businesses.
The investment is centred on the R15.2bn development of Bokoni Platinum Mines in Limpopo and a R753m project to resume open-pit mining and nickel concentrate production at Nkomati in Mpumalanga, which has been on care and maintenance since 2021.
The Bokoni project will expand the mine’s processing capacity to 180,000 tonnes a month in phases, combining a refurbished 60,000-tonne-a-month plant with a new 120,000-tonne plant. First production from the refurbished plant is scheduled for the first half of the 2028 financial year, and the new plant is expected to follow in the second half of the 2030 financial year.
ARM expects Bokoni to produce 350,000 to 400,000 ounces of PGMs a year once it reaches full production in 2032.
ARM estimates the Bokoni project will take just over six years to recoup its investment, based on its projected costs and long-term PGM price assumptions.
ARM has approved the resumption of open-pit mining and nickel production at Nkomati, which is expected to operate for 13 years and produce about 56,000 tonnes of nickel concentrate a year at full production. The concentrate is material processed from mined ore to increase its nickel content before further refining.
ARM expects the Nkomati project to repay its investment in just more than five years. The nickel concentrate offtake agreement with Swedish miner Boliden has yet to become unconditional.
The projects come as ARM, valued at about R31bn on the JSE, reported a 19% increase in headline earnings to R3.2bn for the year to end-June. The improvement was mainly driven by higher PGM prices in dollar terms, partly offset by lower iron ore prices in rand terms and reduced local sales volumes at the Beeshoek mine in the Northern Cape, which was placed on care and maintenance in October last year.
ARM ended the financial year with net cash of R10.2bn, up from R6.6bn a year earlier, and declared a total dividend of R12 a share, compared with R10.50 a year earlier.
The earnings recovery was uneven across its portfolio. ARM Platinum returned to profit, with headline earnings of R1.35bn after a loss of R1.29bn a year earlier, and Two Rivers and Modikwa, both in Limpopo, recorded improved earnings as higher PGM prices supported revenue.
By contrast, headline earnings from the group’s iron ore business fell 41% and manganese earnings dropped 68%.
In its commodities outlook, ARM said the medium- to long-term outlook for PGMs remained constructive, noting resilient industrial demand and the potential for tighter supply as ageing mines and underinvestment weigh on production. It acknowledged that rising electric vehicle penetration remains a challenge for automotive demand.
The iron ore outlook was more uncertain. ARM said prices initially rose during the first half before retreating, with the increase driven partly by higher freight and bunker costs amid the US-Iran conflict, rather than stronger underlying fundamentals. Weak Chinese demand and steel output and rising port inventories remained concerns.
Manganese markets face weaker Chinese demand and lower steel and ferroalloy production. Nickel received some price support from Indonesia’s policy changes, though inventories and potential future supply remain risks.
The group said thermal coal prices had benefited from substitution away from expensive liquefied natural gas, but the medium-term outlook remained subdued amid demand, supply and renewable energy trends.

articles.title: Codelco copper mine blockade adds to supply concerns - Mining.com
articles.summary: Codelco copper mine blockade adds to supply concerns  Mining.com
articles.full_text:
Workers at Codelco’s Ministro Hales copper mine in northern Chile blocked access to the operation for about six hours on Monday in a dispute over unpaid bonuses following a serious workplace accident.
Union leaders and employees erected barricades and occupied the main entrances to the state-owned miner’s Ministro Hales Division in Calama, bringing production and vehicle movements to a standstill.
“Safety is at a standstill, and the workers are not receiving their bonuses as they should,” Alberto Muñoz, legislative director of the Federation of Copper Workers, told Cooperativa radio.
The disruption adds to labour unrest affecting major copper operations as demand for the metal grows from power grids, electric vehicles and data centres.
Safety dispute
A recent study by Santiago-based GEM Mining Consulting found that strikes, severe weather, accidents and geological problems put an average 5.2% of production at Chile’s largest copper mines at risk.
The firm’s first Production-at-Risk Index assessed 14 major copper operations across eight threats, with risk scores ranging from 2.6% to 9%. El Teniente ranked highest at 9%, followed by Los Pelambres at 8% and Escondida at 7.5%. Nine operations had at least one threat rated high.
The findings underscore the uncertainty surrounding mine production forecasts, which generally assume operations proceed as planned despite recurring disruptions from labour disputes, equipment failures and other operational challenges.
The dispute at Ministro Hales stems from a December 2025 accident in which a haul truck caught fire, leaving an operator with serious burns.
The incident forced 13 trucks and associated fleets out of service for several days, affecting bonus payments to workers. Union representatives allege that management is making employees bear the financial consequences of inadequate corporate safety practices.
Muñoz said union leaders began occupying the division’s gates at 6 a.m. He warned that protests could spread to Codelco’s Chuquicamata, Radomiro Tomic and Gabriela Mistral operations unless senior management addresses workers’ concerns.
The possibility of further blockades raises the stakes for Codelco, whose operations are central to Chile’s copper industry. Any escalation could affect production beyond Ministro Hales.
Wider disruptions
The Chilean protest comes as more than 1,200 workers at Teck Resources’ Highland Valley Copper mine in British Columbia, Canada’s largest open-pit copper mine, walked off the job on Saturday.
The operation has continued at reduced capacity, adding another potential constraint on copper supplies.
The strike also comes as Teck pursues its merger with Anglo American (LON: AAL), a combination expected to create one of the world’s five largest copper producers.

articles.title: Lucky Group-QatarEnergy Consortium Abandons $2 Million LNG Terminal Project at Port Qasim - Energy Update
articles.summary: Lucky Group-QatarEnergy Consortium Abandons $2 Million LNG Terminal Project at Port Qasim  Energy Update
articles.full_text:
ISLAMABAD: Energas, a consortium comprising Pakistan’s Lucky Group and QatarEnergy, has abandoned its plan to establish a liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminal at Port Qasim, citing changes in national energy policy, unresolved regulatory issues and concerns over the project’s commercial viability.
Thank you for reading this post, don't forget to subscribe!
The development comes as the Port Qasim Authority (PQA) has warned the consortium that its final letter of intent (LOI) could be cancelled unless it provides unconditional acceptance by November 30, 2026, along with an updated project status. The authority has also warned that failure to meet the deadline could result in the forfeiture of the $2 million initial concession fee deposited by Energas.
In response, Energas Chairman Muhammad Ali Tabba has approached Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, seeking a refund of the amount and requesting that the consortium be absolved of contractual liability for delays and its inability to proceed with the project.
Tabba argued that the consortium had undertaken the self-financed project in good faith to meet Pakistan’s energy requirements at the time of its conception. However, he said subsequent changes in national energy needs and persistent unresolved policy and fiscal matters had undermined its viability.
According to Energas, the government had committed to resolving outstanding issues following discussions with Qatar, but key matters remained unresolved, discouraging further investment and preventing the consortium and QatarEnergy from reaching a final investment decision.
Among the outstanding concerns were pipeline capacity allocation, gas transportation agreements with relevant companies, access to the terminal’s tie-in area, exemptions from third-party access requirements and tax incentives.
QatarEnergy had reportedly booked terminal capacity and committed to supplying additional LNG at a price linked to approximately 10.2% of Brent crude prices to support utilisation of the proposed facility. However, the project failed to progress amid changing market conditions and continuing disagreements over the regulatory framework.
Energas also cited Pakistan’s Integrated Energy Study, whose final report was issued on March 28, 2025. According to the consortium, the study indicated that no additional LNG terminals would be required over the following five years, significantly weakening the economic rationale for the proposed investment.
The consortium further highlighted changes to the tax regime. Under Pakistan’s LNG Policy 2011, terminal operators had been eligible for a five-year tax holiday beginning from the commercial operations date. However, the exemption was withdrawn for new terminals in June 2021, while existing beneficiaries continued to enjoy the facility. Energas attributed the change to conditions imposed by the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
The project was initially conceived when Pakistan was seeking to expand its LNG import infrastructure. However, the country’s energy requirements subsequently changed, with authorities seeking to divert existing contracted LNG cargoes amid shifting demand and supply conditions. Disruptions associated with tensions involving Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz further complicated the LNG supply outlook.
Pakistan had also amended its LNG policy ahead of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s visit to Qatar in August 2022, aiming to remove restrictions on new private-sector terminals supplying part of their capacity to the government and encourage further cooperation with Qatar.
Despite these efforts, the proposed terminal remained stalled for approximately three years.
The PQA, however, has rejected the consortium’s position that the outstanding matters justify its failure to proceed. In its correspondence, the authority maintained that the $2 million payment was an initial or partial concession fee under Clause 2.6(i) of the Project Guidelines 2019, rather than a refundable advance.
The authority said the applicable guidelines and the final LOI provided for termination and forfeiture of the amount if the developer failed to fulfil the prescribed conditions or provide unconditional acceptance within the stipulated timeframe, unless otherwise agreed by the parties.
PQA also maintained that arranging project financing, completing technical and environmental studies, obtaining regulatory approvals, securing pipeline access and ensuring compliance with applicable requirements were the developer’s responsibilities.
The dispute places the proposed LNG terminal’s future in doubt and highlights the challenges facing private-sector investment in Pakistan’s energy infrastructure amid changing demand forecasts, regulatory uncertainty and evolving government priorities.
