Strategic partnership supports scalable, cost-effective liquefied natural gas production as global markets pivot toward energy diversification.
The move comes at a time when the U.S. LNG industry is simultaneously navigating political headwinds and accelerating global demand. Despite federal policy uncertainty in 2025—including potential rollbacks of clean energy incentives and infrastructure permitting delays—the sector remains a critical player in supplying reliable energy to regions in transition, including Europe, Asia, South America, and the Middle East.
Supporting LNG Growth with Modular Innovation
At the core of this collaboration is Honeywell’s modular pretreatment technology, including its Mercury Removal Unit (MRU), Acid Gas Removal Unit (AGRU), and patented SeparSIV® Unit. Together, these systems are designed to remove mercury, carbon dioxide, sulfur, water, and heavy hydrocarbons—ensuring natural gas meets stringent LNG specifications.
“Pretreatment is one of the most vital components of LNG production,” said Rajesh Gattupalli, President of Honeywell UOP. “Without it, impurities can reduce plant efficiency, increase maintenance, or cause catastrophic freezing in downstream equipment.”
Unlike traditional systems, Honeywell’s pretreatment technologies offer modularity and flexibility, with the SeparSIV® system boasting up to 50% lower lifecycle costs compared to conventional approaches. Its ability to handle varying feed compositions adds further resilience, a crucial attribute given the shifting supply mix entering LNG terminals.
Argent LNG’s Vision for Scale and Speed
Argent LNG’s proposed facility is ambitious. The initial phase targets 12 million tons per annum (MTPA) of LNG production capacity, with a roadmap to expand to 25 MTPA, potentially ranking it among the world’s largest LNG terminals. Beyond size, Argent is prioritizing speed, opting for modular construction approaches that reduce on-site risk and compress construction schedules.
“Delivering reliable, clean energy to the world means rethinking how we build and operate LNG infrastructure,” said Jonathan Bass, CEO of Argent LNG. “Honeywell’s technologies align with our mission to deploy fast, efficient, and scalable energy solutions.”
Port Fourchon, a longstanding base for offshore energy logistics, offers strategic advantages—including deepwater access and proximity to natural gas basins—making it an ideal launch point for large-scale LNG exports.
Global Market Context and Energy Security
According to the Shell LNG Outlook 2025, global LNG demand is expected to surge 60% by 2040, driven by coal-to-gas switching, industrial decarbonization, and energy diversification. European markets, in particular, continue to seek U.S. LNG to reduce dependency on Russian gas. Meanwhile, growth in South and Southeast Asia reflects a shift toward gas as a transitional fuel in emerging economies.
As political volatility challenges energy diplomacy, technology-led solutions like those offered by Honeywell are becoming central to reshaping how the U.S. can remain a reliable supplier.

articles.title: Petronet LNG to invest Rs 1,200 crore in 10 compressed biogas plants through JV with Gruner - BioEnergy Times
articles.summary: Petronet LNG to invest Rs 1,200 crore in 10 compressed biogas plants through JV with Gruner  BioEnergy Times
articles.full_text:
Petronet LNG is entering India’s compressed biogas (CBG) sector through a proposed joint venture with Gruner Renewable Energy, committing an estimated Rs 1,200 crore to establish 10 plants with a combined production capacity of 180 tonnes per day.
The company has signed a binding term sheet with Gruner to set up the venture on an equal 50:50 ownership basis. Each facility will have a capacity of 18 tonnes per day. The proposed investment marks Petronet’s first major move into large-scale domestic gas production as it looks to diversify beyond its core liquefied natural gas (LNG) business.
The companies have yet to disclose the locations of the proposed plants or their expected commissioning schedules.
The diversification comes amid supply disruptions and price volatility in the global LNG market. Petronet’s Dahej LNG terminal handled 192 trillion British thermal units (TBtu) during the April-June 2026 quarter, down from 207 TBtu in the year-ago period. Disruptions affecting Qatari gas supplies amid restrictions around the Strait of Hormuz contributed to the decline, while higher spot LNG prices underscored the exposure of import-dependent businesses to geopolitical risks.
At full capacity, the 10 CBG plants could produce around 63,000 tonnes annually, assuming 350 operating days. Although this would be small compared with India’s annual LNG imports of approximately 25.5 million tonnes, the project would give Petronet access to the domestic renewable gas market and diversify its sources of revenue.
The proposed CBG investment is part of a broader portfolio of expansion projects. Petronet is investing Rs 20,685 crore in an integrated petrochemical complex at Dahej and developing the Rs 6,355 crore Gopalpur LNG terminal. The latter is expected to increase the company’s regasification capacity by nearly 18% to 32.5 million tonnes annually.
The CBG venture could also benefit from the government’s blending mandate for city gas distribution companies, which requires compressed biogas to be blended with transport compressed natural gas (CNG) and household piped natural gas. The blending obligation is scheduled to increase from 3% in FY27 to 5% from FY29.
However, the project’s execution will depend on the availability of a consistent supply of agricultural and organic waste across the locations where the plants are established. Unlike its LNG operations, which rely on imported cargoes, the proposed business will require a reliable domestic feedstock procurement and supply chain.

articles.title: Which Glencore (ASX:GLC) Copper Moves Matter After Its Debut? - Kalkine Media
articles.summary: Which Glencore (ASX:GLC) Copper Moves Matter After Its Debut?  Kalkine Media
articles.full_text:
Highlights
- Glencore is still settling into life as a dual-style listing on the Australian market.
- Firmer copper and a strong day for miners gave the sector a lift on Tuesday.
- Local interest in the stock is tied closely to the electrification and data centre story.
Glencore (ASX:GLC) GLC (ASX:GLC) is back in focus this week as miners rallied on the Australian market and copper firmed on better sentiment and signs of demand from China. The diversified producer only listed its depositary interests in Sydney recently, and traders are now asking which of its copper-linked moves will matter most to local owners of the stock as it beds in. Glencore sits outside the ASX 200, among the market's smaller listed companies. It is among the key developments in today's ASX Metal and Mining Stocks coverage.
A debut that drew heavy trading
Glencore made its Australian debut earlier this month, listing CHESS depositary interests alongside its existing London and Johannesburg lines. Trading on the earliest day was heavy, with the stock opening firmer before easing and closing a little lower than where it started the session.
That kind of volatility on day an is not unusual for a large secondary listing. Volume tends to be driven by index-style demand and local desks testing liquidity, and the real picture usually emerges over the following weeks as normal trading patterns settle.
Why copper sits at the centre of the story
Management has openly said it hopes Australian participants in resources stocks will pay more attention to its copper exposure. Copper is tied to electrification, grid expansion, transport and the power needs of artificial intelligence data centres, themes that have attracted steady attention from funds.
On Tuesday copper firmed after a recovery in technology shares lifted risk appetite and Chinese import premiums pointed to healthier appetite for the metal. Visible stockpiles in China also drew down as smelters went into maintenance, tightening nearby supply.
The Rio Tinto backdrop
Glencore arrived on the Australian board after merger talks with Rio Tinto ended earlier in the year. That episode left the market with a clear sense that the miner is willing to consider large combinations, and some commentators see the new listing as a way to widen the pool of likely owners.
Where the index question comes in
among the more watched questions is index inclusion. Management has said the company could join the ASX 200 within a year, although some market watchers believe the step could come sooner given its size once converted at prevailing prices.
Inclusion matters because index-tracking funds must carry constituent stocks, which can create steady demand. Until that happens, the register is likely to be shaped by active managers and local institutions rather than passive money.
What a diversified model offers
Glencore is not a pure copper play. Its portfolio spans copper, zinc, nickel, coal and a large marketing arm that trades physical commodities, giving it earnings that do not always move in step with any single price.
For local readers following ASX Metal and Mining Stocks, that mix is a point of difference from smaller copper-focused names. The marketing business can benefit from volatility and dislocation, while the mining side is more exposed to the cycle in each commodity.
Supply signals in copper
The supply side of copper has been mixed. Stockpiles in the London Metal Exchange system rose last week, easing some of the immediate fear of shortage, though much of the metal was in North America, which raised concern about regional bottlenecks.
The strike risk and mine disruptions
Copper supply has also faced disruption elsewhere. A labour dispute at a large Canadian copper operation has been in the news this week, adding to the long list of operational hiccups that keep the market sensitive to unexpected outages.
Macro events the market is weighing
The broader Australian market closed modestly higher, with materials the standout sector and banks weaker. Attention now turns to monthly inflation data due on Wednesday, followed by the next decision from the Reserve Bank in early November.
How the depositary structure works
Depositary interests are a practical device. The underlying shares stay registered offshore, while a local custodian issues interests that trade on the Australian exchange and settle through the domestic clearing system. Local participants get exposure without opening an overseas account.
Why local portfolios care about diversified miners
Australian portfolios have long been weighted to resources, but exposure has been concentrated in iron ore and a handful of large names. A listed copper and zinc producer with trading operations adds a different earnings pattern to a local portfolio.
Risks that come with the territory
Risks are real. Commodity prices can swing quickly, regulatory and political changes in producing countries can affect mining licences, and the marketing arm brings counterparty and trading risk that is harder to model than a simple mine.
Reading the sector tape on Tuesday
Materials led the Australian market on Tuesday, with the sector rising fora sizeable share session running as copper steadied and gold miners also climbed. Energy shares edged up, while the big banks slipped, taking some of the shine off an otherwise positive session for the broader benchmark.
Governance and disclosure questions
Because the listing is a secondary line, the company continues to follow its home-market reporting calendar, with results and production updates released in London before anything else and then lodged with the Australian exchange. Local readers should expect the same documents rather than a separate Australian version.
What the market is watching next
In the near term the watch list is practical: how the depositary interests trade as the register matures, whether copper keeps its advances, and whether any sign emerges of a timetable for index entry. Quarterly production data from the company is also awaited.
None of this changes the underlying business, which remains a global commodity producer and trader. But the Australian listing gives local readers a clearer window into a company that has often been discussed mostly through London headlines.

articles.title: Is the Quarterly Update Reshaping Views on Kinder Morgan (NYSE:KMI) Pipelines? - Kalkine Media
articles.summary: Is the Quarterly Update Reshaping Views on Kinder Morgan (NYSE:KMI) Pipelines?  Kalkine Media
articles.full_text:
Highlights
- Kinder Morgan has published third-quarter materials on its corporate website, including a results release and quarterly filing.
- The business rests on contracted natural gas transmission, products pipelines and terminals across North America.
- Expansion projects, regulation and capital allocation are the recurring themes in the company's quarterly discussion.
Pipeline operators rarely generate dramatic headlines, yet Kinder Morgan (NYSE:KMI) Energy Kinder Morgan Inc (NYSE:KMI) 33.85 USD -0.090 0.265% Last Updated at: 2026-10-27T20:10:00Z is drawing renewed attention as the market digests its newest quarterly reporting cycle. The company runs the largest independent natural gas pipeline footprint in North America, and its results are read as a barometer for how much gas the continent is moving, how full its storage and terminal assets are, and how steadily contracted fees keep arriving. As a constituent of the S&P 500, the stock is also followed by broad-market participants who care less about commodity swings and more about the toll-road character of the business.
The central event is the third-quarter results release and the related regulatory filings. The company's corporate website now lists third-quarter materials, including a results release, a webcast link and a quarterly report filing. This article does not restate figures from those documents. Instead it explains what the company is, why the quarter matters, and which themes stakeholders tend to examine when a midstream giant reports, using only facts that the published sources support.
Market participants frequently monitor Energy Stocks to better understand trends affecting pipeline operators, power generators, exporters and producers, because the same molecules and the same steel link all of them. Kinder Morgan (NYSE:KMI) Energy Kinder Morgan Inc (NYSE:KMI) 33.85 USD -0.090 0.265% Last Updated at: 2026-10-27T20:10:00Z sits at the center of that chain, which is why a routine quarterly update from the company can carry meaning well beyond its own balance sheet.
What Has Put Kinder Morgan Back in Focus This Week?
The immediate trigger is the arrival of the quarterly reporting package. For a company of this scale, a results release is not a single number but a bundle: the press release itself, supplementary tables showing performance by business segment, a webcast where management fields questions, and the formal quarterly report filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The company's corporate website presents these items together, which makes it straightforward to see how the narrative and the regulatory record line up.
What makes the timing interesting is the backdrop. Natural gas has moved from being a background utility input to a strategic subject in conversations about electricity demand, liquefied natural gas exports and industrial reshoring. A pipeline owner that moves a large share of the natural gas consumed in the United States therefore reports into a market that is unusually attentive to volumes and contract renewals.
Because no figures are repeated here, readers should treat the company's own documents as the authority on the numbers. The value of this discussion lies in framing: what to look for, why it matters, and how the quarter fits into the longer story of a business built on regulated and contracted cash flows.
How Does a Pipeline Giant Like Kinder Morgan Actually Earn Its Keep?
The business model is deliberately dull, and that is the point. The company owns pipelines, storage caverns, processing and treating facilities, marine and rail-connected terminals, and a renewable natural gas and carbon dioxide business. Customers pay to reserve capacity or to move product, and in many cases those payments are fixed by long-term contracts regardless of how much commodity price volatility occurs upstream.
Four broad reporting groups organize the enterprise. Natural gas pipelines are the largest by far and include interstate systems such as Tennessee Gas Pipeline, El Paso Natural Gas and Natural Gas Pipeline Company of America, alongside intrastate networks serving Texas. Products pipelines carry refined fuels and condensate. Terminals handle liquids, dry bulk commodities and steel, and sit near ports, refineries and industrial hubs. The carbon dioxide segment, which pairs oil production with carbon dioxide supply, is smaller and more commodity sensitive.
This mix explains why the stock is often described as a bond-like energy name. When the majority of earnings stems from capacity reservation, volume weakness in a given month does not immediately hollow out results. The flip side is that growth must be built the slow way, through expansion projects that go through permitting, construction and commissioning over several years.
Why Does the Gas Transmission Network Matter So Much to the Story?
Natural gas transmission is the engine of the enterprise. The company has said in its public materials that its pipelines transport a very large portion of the gas consumed domestically, linking producing basins in Appalachia, the Permian, the Haynesville and the Rockies with demand centers on the Gulf Coast, the Midwest, the Northeast, California and the Southeast. That reach gives it a say in how gas flows when weather, outages or new plants change the map.
Demand has been reshaped by three forces. Liquefied natural gas export terminals along the Gulf Coast need dependable feedgas, and several of them rely on corridors in which the company has capacity. Power generators are leaning on gas to meet rising electricity use, including load associated with data centers. Industrial and petrochemical users continue to anchor baseline consumption. Each force favors owners of firm transportation rights.
Stakeholders usually check whether capacity is contracted for long periods, whether renewals happen at attractive rates, and whether any pipeline segments face a shortfall. A quiet quarter on those questions is, in itself, a form of good news for a toll-road style operator, even if it makes for unexciting headlines.
What Role Do Expansion Projects Play in the Growth Narrative?
A large part of the equity story is the project backlog. Over recent years the company has talked about expansions designed to carry more gas to export terminals, to power plants and to growing metropolitan areas. These projects typically begin with binding commitments from customers, then move into regulatory review at the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, where environmental studies and public comment periods shape timelines.
The mechanics matter for how the market reads each quarter. When a project reaches construction, capital spending rises before revenue shows up. When a project enters service, the contracted fees begin to flow, and the company can point to completed work as evidence that its backlog is more than a slide in a presentation. Delays or cost changes, on the other hand, draw immediate questions on the webcast.
Because the company has repeatedly described its approach as disciplined, with spending tied to contracts that deliver an attractive payback, stakeholders tend to examine whether new projects meet that standard. Any commentary on in-service dates, inflation in construction costs and the pipeline of new commitments is therefore among the most closely read parts of the quarterly package.
How Do Terminals and Products Pipelines Complement the Gas Business?
While natural gas receives the headlines, the other segments give the enterprise breadth. Products pipelines move gasoline, diesel and jet fuel from refineries to terminals and airports, and their volumes follow driving habits, air travel and industrial activity. Their results tend to be steady, and tariff adjustments allowed by regulators help preserve real revenue over time.
The terminals business is a patchwork of liquids tanks, bulk handling sites and port facilities. Liquids storage benefits when markets are in contango and customers want to store product, and it benefits from long-term leases at hubs along the Houston Ship Channel and the New York Harbor. Bulk terminals handle commodities such as fertilizer, coal, petroleum coke and steel, and respond to trade flows and domestic manufacturing.
Together, these segments diversify the earnings base so that a soft patch in one area is partly offset by strength in another. For equity owners who prefer stability, that diversification is part of the appeal. For those watching for growth, it raises the question of whether terminals can add new capacity in areas where energy export and import patterns are evolving.
What Does the Share Capital Program and Dividend Record Tell Stakeholders?
The company's corporate website highlights several features that bear on capital allocation: an expected annual dividend per share, a multi-billion-dollar program to retire stock, and a notable ownership stake by management, which the company says amounts to a meaningful portion of the equity. It also points to a solid credit standing, a factor that matters because pipeline construction is financed with debt as well as internally generated cash.
Capital allocation in the midstream sector has changed character over the past decade. Earlier, many operators funded growth by issuing new equity and units at regular intervals. Today the emphasis is on self-funding, with distributions covered by cash generation, leverage kept within a defined range, and any surplus directed toward growth projects or toward reducing the share count.
The relevant question for a quarterly update is therefore how the company balances those uses. Stakeholders listen for hints about whether the balance sheet leaves room for acquisitions, whether leverage is moving toward its stated range, and how dividend growth compares with growth in distributable cash. Management ownership adds an alignment signal, since senior executives are exposed to the same share price as other equity owners.

Oct, 27, 2026 Posted by Sylvia Schandert
Week 202644
With no signs that the war in the Middle East will end soon and farmers facing credit restrictions, the crisis in Brazil’s fertilizer industry is worsening. The higher cost of inputs such as sulfur is weighing on demand, which could fall even more sharply than initially expected following the start of the conflict involving the United States, Israel, and Iran.
After reaching a record 49.1 million tonnes last year, fertilizer demand could return to 2022 levels, according to market estimates. Russia invaded Ukraine in early 2022, and both countries are major fertilizer producers. Brazilian demand totaled 41 million tonnes that year. The latest projection reflects delayed purchases and reduced fertilizer application as farmers contend with high costs and tight credit.
In August, the market was forecasting demand of around 45 million tonnes, according to Argus. “The absence of last-minute demand for the 2026/27 soybean planting season and the pace of nitrogen fertilizer imports led market participants to revise their estimates,” said Renata Cardarelli, Argus’s head of agriculture and fertilizer pricing.
In July, five months after the conflict in the Middle East began, the market was less pessimistic and projected a 10% decline in fertilizer demand, as Valor reported.
Since then, demand destruction has intensified, while Brazilian factories have temporarily halted or shut down operations because of sulfur shortages, reducing the supply of phosphate fertilizers. “Taken together, these factors make it reasonable to expect total consumption of less than 42 million tonnes,” said Ana Lígia Lenat, intelligence and projects coordinator at the Brazilian Confederation of Agriculture and Livestock (CNA).
Mosaic has announced temporary or partial shutdowns at five plants in Brazil and reduced output at two blending units. The company estimates that fertilizer deliveries in the country will fall by 10% to 15%, to between 42 million and 44 million tonnes.
Felipe Pecci, Mosaic’s commercial vice president, said 2027 could begin with lower inventories, reduced imports, and domestic production constrained by limited access to sulfur. “It is a concerning and somewhat unprecedented situation for this market,” he said.
Pecci said demand falling below 42 million tonnes in 2026 could not be ruled out. However, that would depend on factors yet to be confirmed, including delayed second-crop purchases, the effects of El Niño, and Chinese restrictions on ammonium sulfate exports.
According to the latest survey by the National Association for Fertilizer Distribution (ANDA), fertilizer deliveries totaled 22.9 million tonnes from January through July, down 8.8% from the same period last year. In July alone, deliveries fell 22.3%, to 3.9 million tonnes.
The table below shows fertilizer import volumes handled at Brazil’s leading ports in the first eight months of the year, according to Datamar data:

Domestic production of intermediate fertilizers totaled 517,000 tonnes in July, down 19.9% year over year. From January through July, production fell 19.7%, to 3.3 million tonnes. According to ANDA, successive increases in sulfur prices in recent months drove the decline. Sulfur is a key feedstock for phosphate fertilizers.
Sulfur prices have fallen 23% over the past seven weeks, according to StoneX, dropping below $1,000 a tonne again. The industry, however, considers the decline insufficient to provide meaningful relief.
“Historically, sulfur cost around $100 a tonne. In October last year, before the war, prices had already reached $600 because of demand associated with the energy transition. The problem is much bigger than the Strait of Hormuz,” said Bernardo Silva, executive director of the National Union of the Fertilizer Raw Materials Industry (Sinprifert).
The forecasts are being revised as the National Supply Company (Conab) projects a 1.4% increase in soybean acreage for the 2026/27 crop—the smallest expansion in 20 years. Brazil is expected to harvest 181.6 million tonnes of soybeans, though concerns remain that El Niño could affect production.
Mauricio Buffon, president of Aprosoja Brasil, said many farmers are drawing on phosphorus reserves accumulated in the soil in previous years—a form of “savings” that allows them to temporarily reduce replenishment. “Obviously, cutting fertilizer use somewhat reduces yields, but it is necessary to get through this period. Otherwise, farmers would take on even more debt,” he said.
High input costs and weaker farmer demand are also affecting company results. On Thursday, Norway’s Yara said third-quarter net income fell 37.8% year over year, to $199 million.
“The challenges in the fertilizer market are undermining industry dynamics and slowing farmers’ purchasing pace. In addition to geopolitical issues, farmers are contending with weak profitability in some crops and credit restrictions,” Diogo Rezende, vice president of sales at Yara Brasil, said in a statement to Valor.

The NYMEX November natural gas contract gained 9.5 cents on Tuesday to $2.697 per MMBtu, recovering from Monday’s settlement at $2.602, its lowest close since April 28. The bounce came on its second-to-last trading day, as short sellers covered positions ahead of Wednesday’s expiration. The move was technical rather than fundamental: November had sat in oversold territory for five straight sessions, the longest such stretch since April, and traders who sold the contract down from above $3.10 earlier in the month locked in profits before the roll.
The rest of the curve told the real story. December futures, which take over as the front month after Wednesday’s settlement, slipped 2 cents to $3.002 at midday and stayed under pressure into the afternoon. On Monday, December broke to a multi-month low at $2.945. The December through March contracts all declined Tuesday, and the winter strip, the average of November through March, sits at its lowest level since 2021. A rally confined to an expiring contract while every winter month falls is the signature of a market that is still bearish on the season ahead.
The physical market confirms the weakness. Next-day gas at Henry Hub in Louisiana traded at $2.52 per MMBtu, its lowest since November 2024. Spot prices and prompt futures have both fallen toward $2.50 to $2.60 in late October, a level that would have seemed unthinkable at the start of the month when December traded above $3.40.
The scale of the slide is clear on the December contract. It traded as high as $3.709 within the past 30 days and changed hands at $3.411 on October 19 before falling to $2.945 on Monday, a decline of 20.6% from the 30-day high. November dropped from $3.117 on October 16 to $2.602 on Monday, a 16.5% fall in six sessions, including a 4.94% plunge on October 23 alone.
Three forces drove the selloff. Weather forecasts call for unusually mild temperatures across the major U.S. heating markets through early November, delaying the start of heating demand. Lower 48 production has rebounded toward its record of 113.3 billion cubic feet per day after hurricane and pipeline disruptions. And LNG export plants, while running near record levels, have little spare capacity to absorb extra supply.
The thesis for this forecast is direct. Natural gas sits in a shoulder-season trap. Record production, much of it associated gas from oil wells drilling hard with crude above $100, meets a weather pattern that refuses to deliver heating demand, while LNG exports are already running near full capacity. December inherits the front-month role at $3.00 with a bearish trend and a market waiting for cold. Until forecasts turn colder, the path of least resistance runs toward $2.80.
The Expiry Mechanics: Why November Bounced and December Did Not
The divergence between November and December on Tuesday is a feature of contract expiration, and understanding it matters for traders rolling positions this week.
The November contract expires at the close of trading on Wednesday, October 28, three business days before the first calendar day of the delivery month. It is physically settled: a long position held through expiration obliges the holder to take delivery of 10,000 MMBtu at Henry Hub, spread across November. Speculators who do not want physical gas must close or roll their positions before the final bell, and that forced activity creates outsized moves in the final sessions.
Short covering drove Tuesday’s November gain. After a 16.5% decline in six sessions and a close at the lowest level since April 28, traders who had shorted November locked in profits rather than carry positions into the delivery period. Their buying lifted November by 9.5 cents. Moves into expiration week tend to be more technical than fundamental, with traders closing short bets or rolling into December in ways that exaggerate price swings.
December did not get the same support. Traders rolling short positions out of November and into December added selling pressure to the new front month even as November rose. December slipped to $3.002 at midday and remained under pressure as bearish weather forecasts dominated. The December contract is now looking for technical support as it prepares to take the front-month role.
The spread between the two contracts reveals the market’s view. December traded roughly 30 cents above November on Tuesday, a contango that reflects the expectation of higher winter demand. That spread pays traders to store gas now and deliver it in December, which supports continued storage injections into November.
History offers a cautionary note for bears. Past monthly rollovers have produced surprising strength in the new front month, as traders who rolled shorts discover the new contract has less selling pressure behind it. Some analysts expect a short counter-trend rally in December after it takes over, though not necessarily in the deferred winter contracts.
For the forecast, the November bounce is noise. The contract that matters from Thursday onward is December at $3.00. Its multi-month low at $2.945 on Monday reaffirmed the downtrend, and the first test for the new front month is whether it holds that level once November’s short-covering support disappears.
Storage: 3,644 Bcf, 1% Above Average After 10 Bullish Prints
The storage picture is tighter than the price suggests, and that tension sets the floor under the market. Working gas in underground storage reached 3,644 Bcf in the week ended October 16, according to the EIA’s weekly storage report, after a net injection of 77 Bcf. Inventories sit 35 Bcf, or 1.0%, above the five-year average of 3,609 Bcf and 152 Bcf, or 4.0%, below last year’s 3,796 Bcf.
The trend has been tightening. The October 16 injection landed on the tighter side of forecasts and marked the tenth consecutive weekly print that came in below five-year norms. The week ended October 9 brought a 67 Bcf injection to 3,567 Bcf, 23 Bcf below the five-year average of 90 Bcf for that week and below the 76 Bcf consensus, narrowing the surplus to 1.3% from 2.0%. The week ended October 2 brought an 85 Bcf build to 3,500 Bcf, above the 79 Bcf estimate but below the five-year norm of 96 Bcf.
The surplus to the five-year average has narrowed from 2% in early October to 1% now. Measured against last year, inventories are 4% lower, a deficit created by record LNG exports that have pulled more gas out of the domestic market.
Regional detail shows where supply is tight. The South Central region, which includes the Gulf Coast storage that feeds LNG terminals, held 1,125 Bcf, 3.4% below its five-year average and 10.0% below last year. Salt-cavern storage, the most flexible and quickly deliverable inventory, held 251 Bcf, 14.9% below the five-year average and 21.1% below a year ago. The Midwest, by contrast, held 1,065 Bcf, 2.0% above average, and the East held 900 Bcf, 2.7% above average.
The salt deficit matters for winter. Salt caverns can be withdrawn quickly during cold snaps, and a 44 Bcf shortfall against the five-year norm leaves the Gulf Coast with less cushion for a sudden demand spike.
The next report arrives Thursday, October 29, at 10:30 a.m. ET, covering the week ended October 23. Forecasts call for a build near 68 Bcf. A print well below that would extend the streak of bullish storage numbers. A print above 75 Bcf would confirm that mild weather is allowing faster refills.
Projections show inventories reaching 3,850 Bcf by the end of October, 2% above the five-year average entering the heating season on November 1.
For the forecast, storage is a floor, not a ceiling. Inventories near normal mean there is no glut to crush prices further, but no shortage to drive them higher until cold weather begins drawing stocks down.
Production: Back Toward 113.3 Bcf/d After the Isaias Dip
Supply is the dominant bearish force, and it is rebuilding. Lower 48 dry gas production hit records of 113.3 billion cubic feet per day in August and September, then dipped in early October as Hurricane Isaias shut in offshore output and pipeline force majeure events constrained flows. Output averaged 111.5 Bcf/d through the first three weeks of October and dropped to an eight-month low near 107.1 Bcf/d on October 13.
The disruptions were temporary. Hurricane Isaias shut in 1.26 Bcf/d of offshore Gulf production on October 9, 58.8% of Gulf offshore gas output. Pipeline problems in Kentucky, Texas, West Virginia and elsewhere cut flows further. As those issues resolved, output recovered. A Columbia Gas Transmission force majeure ended, restoring 1.9 million dekatherms per day of Appalachian pipeline capacity. Output averaged near 113.3 Bcf/d over the past week, matching the August and September records.
Annual numbers show the scale. U.S. gas production reached a record 107.6 Bcf/d in 2025, and federal forecasts call for 112.2 Bcf/d in 2026 and 116.1 Bcf/d in 2027. Year-to-date production through mid-October averaged 4.1% higher than the same period in 2025, putting 2026 on pace for a second consecutive annual record.
Oil is the hidden driver. With Brent near $114 and WTI near $100 on the U.S.-Iran war’s supply shock, oil producers in the Permian and other basins are drilling aggressively. Every barrel of oil from those wells brings associated gas with it, regardless of gas prices. That associated gas, produced as a byproduct rather than because gas prices justify it, is the main source of downward pressure on Henry Hub. Oil-directed rig counts have risen, and gas-directed rigs reached 135 in late September before easing to 133 in the week to October 16, still higher than a year ago.

The U. S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) fell to 282.6 million barrels as of October 23, 2026, the lowest level since October 1982, when reserves stood at 280.8 million barrels. This represents a decline of over 31%-approximately 130 million barrels-since late 2025, when the reserve exceeded 413 million barrels.
The drawdown accelerated following a March 2026 agreement among International Energy Agency (IEA) members to release 400 million barrels to stabilize global prices amid tensions in the Middle East; the U. S. contribution to this volume reached up to 172 million barrels. The government utilized exchange mechanisms, allowing oil companies to withdraw resources with an obligation to return them in larger quantities later. Currently, the rate of withdrawals exceeds the rate of replenishment.
The reserve, consisting of underground salt caverns along the Gulf Coast, now holds roughly 40% of its 714 million-barrel design capacity. For context, the reserve peaked at 726.6 million barrels in January 2010.
While the release of these reserves has increased supply and temporarily capped global price increases, the depleted volume limits the capacity of the U. S. to respond to further supply disruptions. This reduction increases market sensitivity to emergency events, although final pricing remains dependent on OPEC+ production, demand, and commercial storage levels.

This update is being prepared by Addison Mining Services, a London-based consulting firm that was established in 2014 and has completed more than 250 projects for more than 140 clients. Chief Executive Officer and Principal Geologist James Hogg will serve as the Independent Qualified Person (QP) for the report. Hogg has more than 20 years of experience in the mining industry, including preparing NI 43-101 reports for TSX-listed companies. He serves as a QP on porphyry-related deposits and has experience with copper and Mexico.
"Adelita has been materially advanced in less than a year of operations, and we are proud of what our team has delivered," Chief Executive Officer Enrico Gay said. "Updating the technical report ensures the record reflects where the project stands today."
Gay told Streetwise Reports that the company wanted an official, independent document that would provide a record of what it had accomplished during its first 12 months on the project. "We thought this should be done based on our level of activity and advancement on the project," he said. The update also provides a basis for the next milestone.
Algo Grande is planning to be ready to "pull the trigger on an MRE" (mineral resource estimate) on the Cerro Grande skarn by the end of the year, Gay said, "and we felt that updating the 43-101 was the first step."
What the Update Will Cover
Algo Grande drilled four holes for a total of 1,998 meters at the Cerro Grande target during Phase I. A property-wide prospecting campaign was conducted in January 2026, where 49 rock samples were collected. Phase II drilling commenced in June, and approximately 4,000 meters have been drilled in nine holes. In addition to drilling, Algo Grande completed UAV magnetic surveys, mapped the district, and identified the Mezquital porphyry target.
On September 30, Algo Grande entered into a five-year surface access agreement with the Ejido Palos Chinos, which covers approximately 1,796 hectares. Crews commenced a ground gravity survey of approximately 1,296 stations across Mezquital, Cerro Grande, Cerro Potrero, and Las Trancas this month. Hogg visited the project from October 11 to 15 with Vice President of Exploration João Rocha. During their visit, they visited Cerro Grande, Cerro Potrero, Potrero South, Las Trancas, and Mezquital. Hogg also visited the core shack in Navojoa, field operations, and core handling procedures. This visit satisfies the NI 43-101 requirement that the QP personally visit the property.
Algo Grande will file the report on SEDAR+ once completed; however, no completion date was provided. Algo Grande stated that the report has not been completed, and no QP conclusions are expressed or implied.
Algo Grande has drilled nine Phase II holes, but results from only two have been released, according to Gay. "Investors can expect those drill holes to be coming out chronologically to end of year," he said, with Hole 3 expected next.
Cerro Grande Goes Deeper
The 5,895-hectare project lies in the Arizona-Sonora copper belt. Its anchor is the Cerro Grande copper-gold-silver skarn discovery, which shows geophysical continuity along a corridor of more than 7 kilometers. Reprocessed legacy data and mapping point to a possible porphyry system at depth.
On September 11, Algo Grande reported its first Phase II assays. Hole AG-CG-PH2-002 cut 30.23 meters grading 1.5% copper equivalent (CuEq) from 146.70 meters, including 3.55 meters at 9.4% CuEq and 1.20 meters at 15.8% CuEq. The intercept was about 100 meters closer to surface than the Phase I results.
Full results from the hole, released September 23, added a deeper zone of 38.20 meters at 1.0% CuEq from 243.80 meters, about 67 meters below the first. The two zones total 68.43 meters, averaging 1.2% CuEq, assuming 80% metallurgical recovery.
On September 1, Algo Grande closed an oversubscribed private placement of 7,977,497 shares at CA$0.60, raising CA$4,786,498 for exploration at Adelita and working capital.
On October 7, the company said lab tests on drill core showed its copper-bearing skarn is denser than the host rocks, the basis for the gravity survey.
‘Potential for a Giant Discovery'
Bob Moriarty of 321gold.com has covered Algo Grande since the early days. In a September 14 commentary, written before the deeper Hole 2 results came out, he highlighted the 3.55-meter high-grade core of the first reported Phase II hole. Along with the Phase I drilling and the prior operator's results, he said, it shows a system with district-scale potential.
"I have believed since I was first informed about the company that they had the potential for a giant discovery," Moriarty wrote. He added that he thinks the stock is "absurdly underpriced."
In the same piece, he noted that Sonora accounts for about 80% of Mexico's copper output.

articles.title: EU Commission issues evidence call for hydrogen strategy - Enlit World
articles.summary: EU Commission issues evidence call for hydrogen strategy  Enlit World
articles.full_text:
A new hydrogen strategy is proposed for Europe to support the development of a resilient and competitive regional hydrogen value chain
The European Commission has launched a call for evidence and stakeholder consultation on hydrogen in the EU to gather input for a new hydrogen strategy.
The new strategy, intended to replace the first one of 2020, is proposed to address the slower than expected production and use of renewable and low-carbon hydrogen in the EU.
To meet the policy targets, an estimated 3-4Mt of renewable hydrogen is needed by 2030 to fulfil the 10Mt consumption, but the operational capacity is limited and the project pipeline is insufficient to produce this volume.
Currently, the EU consumes between 7-8Mt of hydrogen a year, mainly in refineries and for ammonia production, which remain largely fossil-based.
Renewable and low-carbon hydrogen and derivatives are expected to play an important role in replacing fossil fuel-based input in specific industrial processes that are difficult to decarbonise by means of direct electrification, including refining, steelmaking and chemical production (for example, ammonia for fertilisers and methanol).
They could also contribute to the decarbonisation of aviation and maritime transport through the production of synthetic fuels and other hydrogen-derived fuels.
Also of interest
ALRIGH2T project targets airport hydrogen refuelling
Why the Global Hydrogen Compass points to progress
Slow uptake factors
The Commission has identified several factors for this slow uptake of renewable and low-carbon hydrogen.
These include persistently high costs, with production costs remaining significantly above those of fossil fuel-based alternatives, limited demand, with uncertainties around both long term demand and the development of the hydrogen infrastructure and the limited impact of public support on triggering investment decisions.
Electricity system constraints are another factor, with permitting delays and insufficient renewable and low-carbon generation capacity.
In addition, the international hydrogen landscape is evolving. While the deployment in the EU is slow, greenfield investments are accelerating outside the EU to meet EU demand for low-carbon hydrogen, derivatives and low-carbon products such as sponge iron and e-fuels. This could increase competitive pressure and raise concerns about strategic dependencies and supply diversification.
Hydrogen strategy
The intent of the new hydrogen strategy is to set out a renewed EU approach to hydrogen so that it better supports industrial competitiveness, strengthens energy security and contributes to the achievement of the EU’s 2050 climate neutrality objective, the call for evidence document reads.
Its aim is to set out a clear and credible trajectory for renewable and low-carbon hydrogen by 2030 and beyond to support the development of a European hydrogen value chain, while safeguarding existing decarbonisation investments and providing stability and predictability for investors.
It will also set the trajectory for renewable and low-carbon hydrogen deployment for 2040 based on ensuring that deployment is cost-effective and support is proportionate, while supporting innovation.
To achieve these objectives, the strategy should propose a set of enabling non-legislative actions focusing on priority sectors and applications where hydrogen delivers the highest added value and on enabling conditions throughout the value chain.
Looking at the energy system as a whole, the actions will cover key areas including industrial competitiveness, infrastructure and trade, skills and technological capacity, research and innovation, including for emerging sources such as natural hydrogen, financing, the role of imports and the EU’s position in international hydrogen markets.
Overall, the strategy will aim to better align EU hydrogen policy with market realities and global developments, mobilising investment where hydrogen can deliver the greatest value, while strengthening the resilience and competitiveness of Europe’s hydrogen ecosystem, the document states.
The new hydrogen strategy is due to be developed in parallel with the renewable energy framework for the period to 2040 to ensure that renewables contribute to the achievement of the 2040 EU climate target.
The call for evidence and stakeholder consultation is open until 23 November 2026.

articles.title: Are African green hydrogen projects for Africans? - Dialogue Earth
articles.summary: Are African green hydrogen projects for Africans?  Dialogue Earth
articles.full_text:
September’s Africa Green Hydrogen Summit in Cape Town brought announcements of new funding and projects, but questions remain about green hydrogen’s future.
The gas has the potential to replace fossil fuels and reduce emissions in hard-to-electrify sectors like steelmaking and shipping. African countries are interested both in exporting hydrogen and using it to achieve their own national energy transition targets.
Between 2017 and 2024, of the more than 50 countries and the EU that released hydrogen strategies, eight were African. The Economic Community of West African States also published one.
Much of this interest has in fact stemmed from Europe, which has placed green hydrogen imported from renewables-rich geographies at the centre of its net-zero plans. The 2022 RePowerEU Plan, for example, targets 10 million tonnes of renewable hydrogen to be imported per year by 2030.
This has given rise to claims of “green colonialism” and the formation of new relationships of extraction from the African continent for European benefit. Yet a number of African governments have enthusiastically promoted green hydrogen, and African research institutions started examining the industry’s potential years before the EU set its target.
“There is a high degree of government agency behind this in African countries,” said Alfonso Medinilla, head of climate action and green transition at the European Centre for Development Policy Management, a think-tank based in Maastricht and Brussels.
What is driving the green hydrogen hype in Africa? And could it offer genuine benefits to African economies?
The hydrogen economy
Hydrogen can fuel vehicles, industrial processes and power stations. The green variety is made by splitting water using renewable power via electrolysis. Hydrogen made using gas is known as grey hydrogen, and with coal, black hydrogen.
African countries, such as Morocco and Namibia, are well placed to make green hydrogen due to their abundant solar and wind resources. North African countries in particular enjoy proximity to one of the world’s largest hydrogen markets, Europe.
The continent has the potential to generate 1,000 terrawatts (TW) of solar and wind power, enough to produce more than 45,000 million tonnes of hydrogen per year, according to the International Energy Agency. An African green hydrogen economy could add up to USD 150 billion to the continent’s GDP by 2050, according to the African Green Hydrogen Report published by German developemnt agency GIZ in 2025.
Products made with the gas are already being used in Africa in various industrial applications such as steelmaking, fertiliser production and mining operations. That said, low-emission hydrogen production was equivalent to just 0.2% of the 3.1 million tonnes of hydrogen used on the continent in 2024.
‘Green colonialism’
Both African and European voices have raised concerns about European green hydrogen investments in Africa, with some using the term “green colonialism”. In a 2023 book produced by research and advocacy organisation the Transnational Institute, Hamza Hamouchene defines this as “the extension of the colonial relations of plunder and dispossession … to the green era of renewable energies, with the accompanying displacement of socio-environmental costs onto peripheral countries and communities, prioritising the energy needs of one region of the world over another.”
The socio-economic concerns relating to hydrogen production can include land acquisition, water stress the impacts of desalination, and the export-oriented focus of many European-supported projects.
Saber Ammar, a researcher at the Transnational Institute, tells Dialogue Earth that hydrogen won’t economically benefit producing countries.
“Technical innovation in developing novel electrolysers and related technologies is concentrated in Europe, North America and Asia,” according to a report on green hydrogen by the International Renewable Energy Agency.
Ammar fears that Tunisia will need to import expensive electrolysers and then export the hydrogen manufactured via them “with low added value”. Tunisia aims to produce 8.3 million tonnes of green hydrogen and its derivatives by 2050 of which 6 million tonnes would be for export.
Other critiques say green hydrogen will divert investments from projects to generate renewable power for direct use on the continent. Global Energy Monitor, which maps international energy infrastructure, found that 61% of all prospective utility-scale wind and solar capacity in Africa is earmarked for green hydrogen, mostly for export to Europe.
Some 600 million people in Africa lack access to electricity. Insufficient energy supplies remain a barrier to economic development in many African countries. Among the continent’s major prospective green hydrogen producers, Namibia and Mauritania have electricity access rates of below 60%, according to World Bank figures.
However, the relationship between hydrogen production and electricity availability is not straightforward.
“If you take away the green hydrogen projects, they will not suddenly release a lot of clean energy to the grid because these projects are being developed with the clean power infrastructure directly linked to them,” says Medinilla of ECDPM.
In fact, to be classified as green, the EU requires green hydrogen to be produced from newly developed renewable energy sources, not existing energy capacity.
African agency
For some, the green colonialism narrative does not hold.
“It’s … not as simple as saying the Europeans are telling the Africans to produce green hydrogen for them at their own expense,” says Medinilla.
“[Governments] want to develop this not because they have been told by Europeans [but] because they see a very clear commercial opportunity in the sector.”
Nonetheless, “these concerns [of green colonialism] should not be dismissed outright,” Joseph Mukendwa, the acting head of the Namibian Green Hydrogen Programme, told Dialogue Earth.
“Given historical considerations, they reflect legitimate questions about ownership, benefit sharing, land use, environmental protection, and also local participation.”
There should be more transparency around how the sector is being built, he says. “The key question is not whether the products are exported, but whether Namibians actually get to meaningfully benefit from the industry.”
The benefits of green hydrogen for African economies
Green hydrogen does seem promising for some countries. Derivatives such as “green” ammonia present an opportunity for green industrialisation and sustainable agriculture. Kenya, for example, is looking into green fertiliser production to reduce import dependence.
Countries across the continent are dependent on fertiliser imports, risking food security during geopolitical tensions such as the ongoing Gulf crisis. If planned properly, experts argue that such projects could improve food security and benefit Kenya economically.
Additionally, exports of green hydrogen and its derivatives to high-demand markets such as the EU have been presented as an economic opportunity for producing countries. What follows is the question of how export revenues can be fairly shared within nations, an issue not unique to the hydrogen sector.
Green fertiliser production and hydrogen exports are just two of several opportunities for African countries in the green hydrogen economy. The possibilities for each country interested in green hydrogen can vary. Medinilla says: “We need to go a bit more in depth and have [clearer] propositions and proposals on how to make these sectors work for African economies and African industrialisation.”
“What level of specialisation in certain products can African countries realistically pursue and what are the industrial policy choices that [they] need to be able to position long term?”
Is green hydrogen stalling already?
There are some concerns that Africa’s hydrogen development may be stalling before it has a chance to convey its benefits. The IEA’s Global Hydrogen Review 2026 reports that within the 2030 project pipeline in Africa, only one of 31 projects has so far moved from planning to a firm commitment to build.
Mukendwa said that the Climate Investment Fund’s Industry Decarbonisation Programme has established an illustrative pipeline of 17 green industries projects in Namibia. Building them all would require USD 20 billion, more than the country’s GDP, demonstrating the complexity of the challenge.
Whether or not African green hydrogen projects will materialise and benefit African economies and societies remains uncertain.

Copper has climbed nearly 20% this year and gold is up a flat 0.02%. One of them gets magazine covers. The other is rewiring every AI data centre on the planet.
Nobody throws a parade for copper. It doesn't have gold's safe-haven mythology or silver's industrial-plus-speculative fan base, and yet three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange hit a record $14,858 a tonne on September 9, 2026, and has spent the weeks since trading in a tight band just under that mark, around $14,400 to $14,600 a tonne through mid and late October. Copper futures in the US touched their own record, $6.95 a pound, on September 22. Gold, by contrast, is up just 0.02% on the year after a brief spike above $5,600 an ounce in late January that mostly evaporated within days.
That gap is the story. Copper is having the kind of year that would be front-page news if it were gold or silver: up nearly 20% year to date and more than 46% over the past twelve months, according to data cited by Yellow.com and KuCoin's markets desk. It just doesn't come with the same cultural weight, so it's happening mostly in trade publications and LME order books instead of on cable news.
Start with the mine that fell down. A mudslide at Codelco's El Teniente operation in Chile, the world's largest underground copper mine, knocked out production and rattled a market that was already thin on spare supply. Chilean output matters more than most single-country numbers in commodities: Chile alone accounts for roughly a quarter of global mined copper, so any disruption there moves the whole curve.
Then there's the inventory picture, and it's genuinely tight. LME-registered copper stockpiles have fallen by about 42% so far this year to their lowest levels since 2021, and the cash-to-three-month spread on the exchange has widened to $434 a tonne, matching levels last seen during the 2021 supply squeeze. When that spread blows out, it means buyers who need copper right now are paying a steep premium over copper for later delivery. That is exactly the kind of signal that shows physical metal is scarce, not just expensive on paper.
Copper hit $14,875 a tonne on the LME in September, Glencore cut its 2026 output guidance after mine setbacks in Chile, and Goldman's Jeff Currie says commodities are only in the first inning of a decade-long run. - AI data center copper demand forecast 2025 - Goldman Sachs copper supercycle AI infrastructure buildup
Layer onto that a very American distortion. The Trump administration's Section 232 review was supposed to produce a recommendation on refined copper cathode tariffs by June 30, 2026. That deadline passed with no public determination, and the proposal still on the table would phase in a 15% tariff from January 2027, rising to 30% in 2028. Traders didn't wait for clarity. They just started shipping. An estimated 900,000 tonnes of copper moved into US warehouses in 2026, pushing COMEX stockpiles to a record 675,185 metric tons after 46 consecutive days of gains. Goldman Sachs had to tear up its own forecast midyear, swinging from a projected 490,000-tonne global surplus in April to a 640,000-tonne deficit outside the US by June, once it became clear how much metal was getting parked stateside ahead of a tariff that still hasn't actually arrived.
The AI data centre angle nobody prices in fast enough
Here's the part that should worry anyone treating AI capex as a software story. Fastmarkets' LME Week panel put data centre copper demand at nearly 1 million tonnes, with estimates for the incremental AI-driven slice of that running between roughly 200,000 and 400,000 tonnes in 2026 alone, depending on whether you're counting new demand or total copper embedded in new builds. Every GPU cluster needs enormous amounts of copper wiring and busbar just to move power from the grid connection to the racks, and that demand shows up well before the chips inside ever ship a single token.
Investor Michael Burry, who's made a habit of poking holes in AI enthusiasm, has pointed to the mismatch directly: new copper deposits take roughly 18 years to reach production, while AI data centres can go from groundbreaking to full power draw in two to three years. You cannot permit, build, and ramp a new mine on a timeline that matches a hyperscaler's capex cycle. That gap is structural, not cyclical, and it's why copper's price action is a cleaner read on real AI infrastructure spending than anything in the chip supply chain, where announced orders and actual shipped silicon can diverge for quarters at a time.
Frankly, if you want to know whether the AI buildout is real money moving through real concrete and real substations, rather than just backlog numbers on an earnings call, copper inventories are a better gauge than most of what gets covered. Gold tells you how scared people are. Copper tells you how much is actually getting built.
None of this means copper is risk-free from here. Tariff policy could still resolve in a way that unwinds the US stockpiling trade fast, and a chunk of this year's rally is squarely a function of metal getting hoarded in American warehouses rather than consumed. But the underlying demand story, grid buildout, electrification, and a data centre boom that needs copper years before it needs more chips, isn't going away once the tariff noise settles. The boring metal just keeps setting records while everyone watches gold.

- Li-FT Power Ltd. (TSXV:LIFT) experienced downward pressure as investors assessed weaker lithium prices, development-stage valuations and uncertainty surrounding future project economics.
- Recent drilling results from the Adina-Galinée Lithium Project indicate continued mineral exploration progress, although resource development, financing and commercialization remain important challenges.
- Exposure to Canadian lithium resources and potential battery supply-chain expansion offers longer-term opportunities, but commodity volatility and execution risks warrant a cautious near-term outlook.
Li-FT Power Ltd. (TSXV:LIFT) is a Canadian mineral exploration and development company focused on hard-rock lithium assets. Its principal projects include the Yellowknife Lithium Project in the Northwest Territories and the Adina-Galinée Lithium Project in Quebec. Despite continued exploration activity and strategic expansion, the stock remains sensitive to lithium market weakness, development costs and changing investor expectations. Uncertain electric vehicle demand growth, global lithium supply conditions and financing requirements further complicate the near-term outlook.
Why Did Li-FT Power Ltd. (TSXV:LIFT) Fall by 4.76% on 26 October, 2026?
Li-FT Power Ltd. (TSXV:LIFT) declined by 4.76% to CAD 1.40 on 26 October 2026, according to the supplied trading figures, indicating notable selling pressure.
The decline coincided with the company's announcement of initial drilling results from its Adina-Galinée Lithium Project in Quebec. Although the results confirmed additional lithium mineralization, investors may have remained cautious about commodity prices, development expenditure and future project profitability.
The broader lithium sector has faced pressure from weaker spodumene and lithium carbonate prices. Such conditions can reduce confidence in development-stage projects, even when exploration results are encouraging.
The business model of Li-FT Power Ltd.
Li-FT Power acquires, explores and advances lithium-bearing mineral properties, primarily targeting spodumene deposits.
Its Yellowknife Lithium Project contains multiple lithium-bearing pegmatite systems, while the Adina-Galinée project provides additional exposure to Quebec's emerging battery minerals industry.
The company seeks to create value through drilling, resource definition, metallurgical testing, feasibility studies and eventual project development.
Potential future revenue would depend on successful lithium concentrate production, processing arrangements or strategic commercial partnerships.
As an exploration-stage business without established commercial mining operations, Li-FT remains dependent on capital markets and disciplined project advancement.
Key Reasons Behind Decline
Lithium Commodity Price Weakness
Lower lithium prices can reduce expected project returns and weaken investor appetite for emerging producers. Persistent commodity weakness may also complicate financing discussions.
Development and Execution Uncertainty
Li-FT must advance technical studies, environmental assessments and project planning before commercial production becomes feasible. Delays could increase costs and postpone potential revenue.
Capital Requirements
Large-scale lithium development requires significant investment in processing infrastructure, transportation and mine construction. Additional financing may introduce dilution or borrowing obligations.
Electric Vehicle Demand Concerns
Although battery demand presents long-term opportunities, slower electric vehicle adoption or changes in battery technology could affect lithium demand expectations.
Geopolitical and Inflationary Pressure
US-Iran tensions and broader geopolitical instability could increase fuel, equipment and transportation expenses. Higher development costs may offset potential benefits from strategic demand for Canadian critical minerals.
Recent Corporate Developments
Adina-Galinée Drilling Results
On 26 October 2026, Li-FT announced initial assay results from its summer drilling program at the Adina-Galinée Lithium Project. The reported intersections demonstrated continued spodumene mineralization and provided additional geological information for resource evaluation.
Renard Infrastructure Opportunity
The company recently satisfied conditions associated with its option to acquire the former Renard diamond mine site. Access to existing infrastructure could potentially reduce future development requirements, although economic benefits depend on technical assessments and successful execution.
Yellowknife Project Advancement
Li-FT continues evaluating its Yellowknife lithium resources through exploration, metallurgical assessment and environmental baseline work.
These developments support project advancement but do not eliminate commodity-price or commercialization risks.
Risks Investor Needs to Consider
- Commodity risk: Weak lithium prices could undermine project economics.
- Financing risk: Future development may require substantial additional capital.
- Execution risk: Technical challenges could increase construction costs.
- Regulatory risk: Environmental permitting may affect development timelines.
- Market risk: Changes in battery demand could influence lithium pricing.
- Liquidity risk: Speculative selling may amplify short-term share-price volatility.
What Is the Dividend Outlook?
Li-FT Power does not have an established regular dividend-paying profile.
Its capital allocation priorities focus on exploration, technical studies, environmental assessments and potential development infrastructure.
Given the company's pre-production status, preserving liquidity and advancing mineral assets remain more relevant than recurring shareholder distributions.
What Does the ESG Investment Case Look Like?
Environmental considerations: Lithium mining requires careful management of land disturbance, water resources, waste materials and energy consumption.
Social considerations: Indigenous engagement, community consultation, worker safety and local employment opportunities remain important for Canadian mining projects.
Governance considerations: Transparent resource reporting, disciplined financing, environmental compliance and responsible capital allocation are essential.
Effective sustainability practices could improve project acceptance, while permitting challenges may create additional expenses.

Bull Case
- Continued drilling success may improve mineral resource confidence.
- Canadian critical minerals initiatives could support development opportunities.
- Existing infrastructure near Adina-Galinée may improve future project economics.
- Growing battery storage demand could support long-term lithium consumption.
- Strategic partnerships may strengthen financing and commercialization prospects.
Bear Case
- Persistent lithium price weakness could reduce expected project returns.
- Development expenditure may increase funding requirements.
- Permitting delays could postpone commercialization.
- Competitive global lithium supply may constrain pricing.
- Weak investor sentiment could sustain valuation pressure.
Technical Levels to Watch
- Support Zone: Recent trading lows may provide an indication of potential buying interest.
- Resistance Levels: Previous recovery areas could attract renewed selling.
- Volume Trends: Elevated selling participation may indicate continued distribution, while improving buying activity could support stabilization.
- Momentum Indicators: Moving averages and relative strength indicators may help assess whether downward momentum is moderating.
Outlook
Li-FT Power Ltd. (TSXV:LIFT) retains longer-term opportunities through its Canadian lithium portfolio, exploration progress and potential infrastructure advantages.
However, near-term performance remains sensitive to lithium prices, financing availability, technical study outcomes and regulatory approvals.
Continued drilling success could improve project confidence, but sustainable valuation recovery will likely require clearer development economics and improved commodity-market conditions.
The outlook remains cautious amid global supply uncertainty, geopolitical developments and capital-intensive project requirements.

The LNG carriers market is shaped by fluctuations in vessel construction costs, shipyard capacity, charter rates, and the availability of specialized containment technologies. This expansion is strengthening the need for LNG transportation capacity, encouraging shipowners to invest in new carriers to connect growing export volumes with international markets.
LNG carriers require substantial upfront investment due to specialized cryogenic cargo containment systems, advanced propulsion equipment, stringent safety requirements, and complex vessel engineering. Construction costs can reach hundreds of millions of dollars per vessel, while lengthy building timelines and limited availability of specialized shipyards increase financial and operational risks. These high capital requirements create barriers for new market entrants and smaller shipowners, potentially delaying fleet expansion and limiting investment in new LNG transportation capacity.

Key Highlights
- Stock Performance: Vizsla Copper Corp closed the October 26, 2026 session down -3.49%, as exploration stage copper equities met renewed selling.
- Project Pipeline: The company's portfolio of British Columbia porphyry projects and an Alaskan VMS asset keeps investor focus on drilling outcomes.
- Copper Demand Debate: Changing views on industrial demand and supply growth continue to drive swings in copper exploration valuations.
- Funding Watch: Multiple active projects require sustained exploration budgets, keeping financing considerations in view for shareholders.
Introduction
Vizsla Copper Corp (TSXV:VCU) is a copper focused exploration and development company with a portfolio of projects in central British Columbia and southeast Alaska. In British Columbia, the Woodjam Project hosts the Deerhorn deposit, which carries a historical resource, while the Poplar Project, covering roughly 44,200 hectares, includes the Poplar copper gold deposit and the Thira target located about 10 kilometres to the south. The company also holds the Palmer Project in southeast Alaska, a volcanogenic massive sulphide property. Across its portfolio, the company targets porphyry copper gold systems and reports copper, gold and silver results.
On October 26, 2026, the shares fell -3.49%, mirroring the uneven trading that has characterized junior copper explorers. Although long term demand narratives for copper remain widely discussed, exploration companies remain highly sensitive to shifts in sentiment, metal price movements and the timing of drill results. With several projects at different stages, Vizsla Copper's valuation depends heavily on the market's confidence in its ability to convert targets and historical resources into modern, economically meaningful deposits. When investors become more risk averse, that confidence can be discounted quickly. Seasonal factors also play a role, since field programs in British Columbia are concentrated in the warmer months, and the transition toward winter can coincide with quieter news flow while assays and interpretation work are completed.
Key Reasons Behind Decline
A combination of sector dynamics and company stage factors appears to explain the latest decline.
- Volatile Copper Sentiment: Copper prices respond to evolving expectations for manufacturing activity, infrastructure spending and electrification. Even modest changes in those expectations can trigger sharper moves in exploration equities, which act as leveraged plays on the metal.
- Waiting for Drill Results: Exploration share prices often rise ahead of drilling and soften as investors wait for assays. Periods between results can see holders reduce positions, particularly if broader market conditions are uncertain.
- Historical Resource Considerations: The Deerhorn deposit carries a historical resource, which the market treats with caution until it is verified and updated to current reporting standards. That uncertainty can limit the value investors are willing to assign.
- Portfolio Funding Demands: Advancing several projects simultaneously requires meaningful exploration spending. The likelihood of additional financing to support these programs can weigh on sentiment, given the potential for dilution.
- Macro and Geopolitical Headwinds: Global geopolitical tensions, trade and tariff uncertainty and energy market volatility have encouraged investors to favour lower risk holdings. Small capitalization explorers are often among the first positions reduced in such environments.
Risks to Consider
The company's prospects should be considered alongside several important risks:
- Exploration Uncertainty: Drilling at Poplar, Woodjam, Thira or Palmer may not deliver results that support resource growth or development, which could weigh on valuation.
- Resource Verification: Historical resources must be confirmed and updated, and there is no assurance that future estimates will match historical figures.
- Financing and Dilution: Funding a multi project portfolio may require repeated equity raises, potentially diluting existing shareholders during weak markets.
- Permitting and Stakeholder Engagement: Projects in British Columbia and Alaska require permits and constructive relationships with Indigenous communities and local stakeholders, which can affect timelines.
- Metal Price Exposure: A sustained decline in copper, gold or silver prices could reduce investor interest in exploration projects and pressure the shares.
Valuation Perspective
From a valuation perspective, Vizsla Copper is assessed on the discovery and resource potential of its project pipeline rather than on cash flow. Investors typically weigh the size and grade of identified mineralization, the stage of technical work and the jurisdiction when assigning value to exploration companies. The company's position in central British Columbia, a region with established porphyry deposits and mining infrastructure, provides context that can support interest, while the Alaskan asset adds further optionality. Because each project sits at a different stage, the market effectively values a basket of opportunities, and the weight assigned to each can shift as new information emerges from the field.
The recent pullback suggests investors are applying a more cautious view until the company delivers results that demonstrate scale and continuity. Valuation could improve with the release of drill results that extend mineralization, progress in updating historical resources to current standards or evidence that multiple targets can be advanced efficiently. Conversely, disappointing results or financing on unfavourable terms could keep the equity under pressure. As with most explorers, share price movements are likely to track news flow and sector sentiment closely.
Outlook
Looking further ahead, structural demand for copper linked to electrification, energy transition and grid investment continues to support interest in well located porphyry projects. Vizsla Copper's portfolio across several projects gives it multiple pathways to potential discovery and resource growth, which may appeal to investors seeking exposure to future copper supply in North America. Successful exploration could also attract interest from larger industry participants looking to replenish project pipelines.
In the short term, however, the shares are likely to remain sensitive to copper price trends, the timing and quality of drill results and broader appetite for junior resource equities. Macroeconomic uncertainty and geopolitical tensions may continue to drive volatility. Until the company provides greater clarity on resource potential and development pathways, trading could remain prone to declines such as the October 26, 2026 move. Investors are therefore likely to watch the cadence of company updates closely in the months ahead.

articles.full_text:
The city-state, which relies on natural gas to generate about 95% of its electricity, is also studying the feasibility of a third LNG import terminal on the northeastern island of Pulau Tekong, Gan said at the Asia Gas Markets conference on Tuesday.
The moves come as Singapore prepares to expand its gas-fired power generation capacity. On Monday, the government said it would add five new gas-fired power plants to raise its electricity generation capacity by around 26% early next decade from around 12 gigawatts at present.
Gan did not provide additional details on GasCo's procurement exercise or the size of the potential third import terminal.
GasCo, which was established in 2025 to centralise Singapore's gas procurement and supply, previously said it would seek long-term LNG supplies in the first quarter of this year for delivery from 2028 onward, moving to secure multi-year contracted volumes rather than relying on one-off spot purchases.
Earlier this year, Singapore also started construction of its second LNG import terminal with a regasification capacity of 5 million tons per annum (mtpa). The project, scheduled to begin operations by 2030, will raise Singapore's total regasification capacity to 15 mtpa.
Separately, Singapore appointed Keppel Energy, Sembcorp Utilities and Tuas Power as aggregators to test the commercial viability of importing and using biomethane for power generation and industrial decarbonisation, Gan said.
"This could open up new opportunities for the gas industry to develop regional biomethane supply chains, leverage existing gas infrastructure and trading capabilities," she added.
